His letter to Speaker John Boehner dated March 16, 2015, stated that he was resigning in order to focus on his existing committee assignments and serve his constituents more effectively. This contradicts Gallego's claim that Hurd said he was unable to find the time to serve. Additionally, evidence from the Congressional Record and other sources shows that Hurd had a valid reason for leaving the committee, citing his multiple assignments and desire to focus on serving his district.

journalist_explanation: AIF rolled out a big ad campaign to combat SB 1832, saying the insurance industry’s "working tax cut" created "over 40,000 new jobs in just the last four years." The problem is the number, which is cherry-picked and wrong. And even if the jobs number was right -- and again, it's not -- experts say the tax cut would only be one factor in a company's decision to expand operations in Florida. We rate AIF's claim Pants on Fire!
generated_explanation: According to evidence from the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation's reports and data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the insurance industry in Florida lost jobs between 2007 and 2010, and at most gained 100 new jobs between 2007 and 2010. This contradicts AIF's claim that the "working tax cut" created over 40,000 new jobs in just the last four years.

journalist_explanation: The claim that the Obama administration has issued rules for "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" is ridiculous; the administration has simply set a floor for how much money per month of the premiums paid by those who have chosen plans that include abortion must be placed in a segregated account in order to make sure that there’s enough money available to pay for abortion services incurred by people enrolled in that plan. The bigger charge -- that the Obama health care law "requires all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay a separate premium from their own pockets to fund abortion" -- is also incorrect. The provision in question only affects people who purchase insurance plans that cover abortion and who do so on the exchanges -- a much narrower group than the claim suggests. And people who make such purchases will be paying their private dollars into abortion coverage accounts voluntarily. Despite some puzzling wording, ultimately the law allows for full disclosure of its abortion rules at the most obvious time, when someone is signing up for coverage. On balance, we rate this claim False.
generated_explanation: The claim of "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" is false because it misinterprets the actual meaning of the $1 figure. According to the evidence, this amount refers to the minimum premium that insurers must allocate per beneficiary into the abortion account, not the cost of an abortion itself. Additionally, while some plans on the exchanges may include abortion coverage and require individuals to pay a separate premium for it, it does not apply to all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage as the claim suggests.

journalist_explanation: Mook wrote, "In last week’s debate, Bernie questioned Hillary’s commitment to fighting climate change because a whopping 0.2 percent of the money given to our campaign has come from employees of oil and gas companies. Not even 2 percent, mind you: 0.2 percent." Mook’s statement is accurate, though it’s carefully constructed to exclude donations by lobbyists who have at one time represented the industry -- a point made by Sanders, though its relevance is up for debate. The statement is accurate but needs additional information, so we rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that Hillary Clinton's campaign did receive a significant amount of money from employees of oil and gas companies, with 0.17% of total donations coming from them. However, the article raises caveats about this statistic, pointing out that Mook excluded other relevant donations, such as those from lobbyists with ties to oil and gas interests. The Sanders campaign argues that these additional donations would bring the total amount received from oil and gas interests closer to 0.8%. While there is evidence supporting both claims, it cannot be determined for certain which one is true based on the provided information.

journalist_explanation: Bachmann said, "a report just came out that if we continue with President Obama's policies, we're looking at over 9 percent unemployment next year in the fourth quarter." But that jobless rate is based a projection of "current law," which would only happen as a result of a standoff between Congress and the president, not Obama’s own policy priorities. Unemployment would rise in the face of immediate deficit reduction — something that more closely resembles Bachmann’s preference than the president’s.The 9 percent unemployment figure is mentioned in the CBO study, but it is inaccurate for Bachmann to say it is under Obama's policies. We rate the claim False.
generated_explanation: The claim states that continuing President Obama's policies would lead to over 9 percent unemployment in the fourth quarter next year, but according to the evidence from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report, this projection is based on current laws being left unchanged, not on continuing President Obama's policies. However, it is also noted that if lawmakers and the president work out a deal that keeps tax cuts and avoids automatic spending cuts, the unemployment rate will actually drop to 8 percent, which is closer to Obama's policy goals. Therefore, it cannot be determined for certain whether the claim is true or false based on the evidence provided.

journalist_explanation: The Facebook post claims Melania Trump removed the roses planted by her predecessors going back to 1913. That’s wrong. Over the years, roses have both died and been replaced as different administrations have left their mark on the White House Rose Garden. Only about a dozen rose bushes remained before this most recent renovation. We rate this Facebook post False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided indicates that the Rose Garden was renovated under Melania's direction, but it was done to address maintenance and drainage issues, as well as to make the garden more accessible. According to landscape historian Marta McDowell, roses are living things and can die off or need to be replaced over time, which supports the claim that the renovation involved replacing old plants with new ones rather than removing historic roses from every First Lady since 1913.

journalist_explanation: U.S. Rep Annie Kuster said the Republican-backed bill she voted for wouldn't pause the resettlement of Syrian refugees. While a number of House Democrats agree with her, the White House and Republicans believe the contrary, saying the bill would either slow down or stop the flow of refugees. Although there’s nothing in the bill that says it will specifically cause a pause, a reasonable reading of the legislation could lead to such an interpretation. Kuster’s claim ignores critical evidence that could lead to an opposite conclusion. We rate her statement Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided contains conflicting statements regarding whether the SAFE Act would "pause" the resettlement of Syrian refugees in the United States. On one hand, Rep. Annie Kuster stated that the bill does not pause the program and that it requires only an extra certification stamp to move forward with admitting refugees. On the other hand, multiple sources including the White House, U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch, and FBI Director James Comey suggest that the bill would create significant delays in the fulfillment of the refugee program. Additionally, supporters of the bill have also referred to it as requiring a "pause" in admitting Syrian and Iraqi refugees while a new vetting process is established.

journalist_explanation: At a news conference, Christie claimed Ronald Reagan "was behind in the polls in 1980 going into the debate with Jimmy Carter and then turned around 10 days later and won 40 states."Reagan went on to win 44 states, but it was not necessarily the comeback victory described by Christie. Reagan was behind in some polls and ahead of Carter in others. Given the margins of error for the polls, the race was "too close to call" and a "virtual dead heat," articles show.We rate the statement Half True.  To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: Although some polls showed Jimmy Carter with a slight advantage over Ronald Reagan in the days leading up to their debate on October 28, 1980, other polls had Reagan ahead or indicated that the race was too close to call due to margin of error. Given this conflicting information, it cannot be determined for certain whether Reagan was truly "behind in the polls" going into the debate.

journalist_explanation: Jerven said that for 21 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, "we simply do not have data to say anything about trends in poverty." His number comes directly from a careful vetting of poverty surveys by the World Bank. That analysis described in detail the holes in the information needed to track poverty. Jerven pushed his point a bit too far by saying that we can’t say anything about trends. Alternative methods give a reasonably reliable picture of overall trends, even if they can’t tell policy makers what the actual poverty rate might be. But at the end of the day, the consensus among the experts we reached is that the gap Jerven talked about is real and rather than use workaround techniques, everyone would prefer solid data. We rate this claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: According to the World Bank, for 2012 only 27 out of 48 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa had conducted at least two comparable surveys since 1990 to track poverty. This aligns with Jerven's statement that "we simply do not have data to say anything about trends in poverty" for at least 21 countries. The World Bank also identifies issues with the data points, including problems with matching and consistency, which supports Jerven's contention that the data behind claims of poverty reduction is suspect.

journalist_explanation: Patrick said Texas this year will "have more money in reserve than the other 49 states combined." On our inquiry, Patrick acknowledged this was a misstatement. Indeed, what he celebrated turned out to be incorrect and ridiculous. Pants on Fire! PANTS ON FIRE – The statement is not accurate and makes a ridiculous claim. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided indicates that while Texas has a significant amount of money in reserve funds, the sum total of reserves in other states is not less than $8.5 billion (the amount cited by Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick). According to multiple sources, including the National Association of State Budget Officers and the Pew Charitable Trusts, the 50 states together are projecting around $53 billion in 2015 fiscal-year-end reserves, with Texas accounting for about $10-11 billion and Alaska accounting for over $10 billion. Additionally, other states such as California, New York, Ohio, Massachusetts, Florida, and Indiana have a combined total of reserves that is greater than Texas'. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that Texas has more money in reserve than the other 49 states combined.

journalist_explanation: Barry Hinckley, in raising questions about whether the United States should be giving foreign aid to countries such as Egypt, said that 80 percent of Egyptians oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.A Gallup poll taken in February shows that he's right in the ballpark.We rate his statement as True.(Get updates from PolitiFact Rhode Island on Twitter: @politifactri. To comment or offer your ruling, visit us on our PolitiFact Rhode Island Facebook page.
generated_explanation: According to two independent polls conducted in Egypt, one by Gallup between Jan. 31 and Feb. 7 with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points, and another by the Pew Research Center from March 19 to April 10 with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points, more than 80 percent of Egyptians do not oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.

journalist_explanation: The Facebook post says Harvard scientists say the coronavirus is "spreading so fast that it will infect 70% of humanity this year." An epidemiologist at the university has said that 40% to 70% of the world’s adult population could be infected in the coming year. But that is a projection, and other projections vary. We rate this post Half True.
generated_explanation: The claim states that Harvard scientists predict 70% of humanity will be infected this year, but Mark Lipsitch, an epidemiologist at Harvard’s Center for Communicable Disease Dynamics, estimates that 40% to 70% of the world’s adult population could be infected in the coming year, not specifically "this year". This difference in language is significant, as it implies a timeline, and without further clarification from other sources, this claim appears to be an exaggeration or misrepresentation of Lipsitch's statement.

journalist_explanation: : Dudgeon’s on target with his claim that the vast majority of states have an appointed state school superintendent. We rate his statement True.
generated_explanation: According to evidence provided by the Council of Chief State School Officers and the Education Commission of the States, 37 states have appointed superintendents, while only Georgia, Wyoming (which is considering switching), and 12 other states have elected superintendents.

journalist_explanation: In a TV ad, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce says Baldwin supports raising taxes by $858 billion, citing her vote against a bill that primarily contained tax cuts.It’s true that had Baldwin’s side prevailed and if no other action was taken, taxes would have increased, although not by the full $858 billion.But Baldwin did vote separately for a measure that would have extended most of the Bush tax cuts. And it can’t be assumed that the Bush tax cuts would not have been extended had the bill Baldwin opposed not become law.There’s only an element of truth in the chamber’s claim, which is our definition for Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The claim is based on a misleading interpretation of Rep. Tammy Baldwin's vote against an $858 billion bill that extended the Bush-era tax cuts. While it is true that the bill added nearly $858 billion to federal budget deficits over 10 years, this figure includes not only the extension of the tax cuts but also other measures such as a new payroll tax cut and the extension of unemployment benefits. Baldwin's vote against the bill does not necessarily mean she supports raising taxes by $858 billion. In fact, she had previously voted for an alternative bill that would have extended the Bush tax cuts permanently for families earning less than $250,000.

journalist_explanation: Freitas says, "VA Democrats authorized for early release over 4,000 inmates, 60% of which are incarcerated for violent offenses." He’s talking about a budget amendment the Democratic-run legislature muscled through at Northam’s request to combat a COVID-19 outbreak in prisons. Freitas’ numbers are good, but his statement lacks context. He didn’t mention - in his Facebook post or during his town hall broadcast - that all of these inmates will be less than a year away from finishing their sentence. They’ll getting out soon anyway, regardless of whether they’re granted early release. So we rate his statement Mostly True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, 4,446 inmates would be eligible for early release (2,761 of whom are classified as violent offenders), whereas Freitas claimed it was 4,000. Additionally, he stated that 60% were incarcerated for violent offenses, but according to the Department of Corrections' classification, only 62% of the eligible inmates are considered violent offenders under parole abolition laws.

journalist_explanation: Pence said, "Today, there are more Hoosiers going to work than ever before in the 200-year history of the great state of Indiana." Literally, Pence has a point: More Indiana residents are employed now than at any time in the past. But it’s a data point with very little meaning, since, as any statistician will tell you, it doesn’t take into account the size of the state’s population. Looking instead at the percentage of Hoosiers working shows that the percentage was higher during the previous employment peak in 2000. And the widely used unemployment rate — which is even more precise because it is based on the number of residents who are actively looking for a job — has been lower than its current rate over long stretches of recent history. We rate the statement Half True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided, while it is true that more Hoosiers are working today than ever before in terms of raw numbers (3.07 million in May 2016), when looking at the percentage of Indiana's population that is working, a bigger percentage was working in 2000 (49.7%) compared to 2016 (47.3%). Additionally, when considering only residents between the ages of 18 and 64, the prime working years, the comparable figure in 2000 was also higher than in 2016.

journalist_explanation: Freitas’s ad says Spanberger and other Democrats "voted to spend public funds on their political campaigns; up to $5 million..." The claim refers to votes Spanberger and 233 of her Democratic House colleagues cast on March 8, 2019 for a bill that would provide a 6-to-1 match on small-dollar contributions to congressional candidates. Bloomberg News estimates candidates could receive as much as $5 million apiece in federal support. Although the bill would be a step towards public financing of congressional campaigns, Freitas glosses over some important details: Participation in the program would be optional, and against the interests of many Democratic and Republican candidates. To be eligible for the match, candidates would have to refuse aggregate contributions from any individual of more than $1,000. The program would not receive tax dollars paid by individuals and households. It would be funded by a 2.75 percent surcharge on civil and criminal fines paid by banks and corporations. Freitas’s statement tells half the story, and we rate it Half True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided, the For the People Act of 2019 would not provide up to $5 million in public financing for a candidate's campaign. Instead, it proposes a matching program that would provide a 6-to-1 match for small-dollar donations ($200 or less), and create a pilot program to provide $25 vouchers for eligible voters to give to their favored candidates for Congress. The funds for the matching program would come from a new "Freedom From Influence Fund" under the U.S. Treasury, which would collect a 2.75 percent surcharge on criminal and civil fines and penalties or settlements with banks and corporations that commit corporate malfeasance.

journalist_explanation: There are two main ways to make this calculation, and they lead to opposite conclusions. While we believe that including payroll taxes in the calculation offers a more accurate picture of what the American public pays the IRS, it's also true that the Obama ad didn't specify which measurement it was using, and in fact used a figure for Romney -- 14 percent -- that was based on income taxes alone. On balance, then, we rate the claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The article presents evidence that the claim is false when considering only income taxes. According to a study by the Urban Institute-Brookings Institution Tax Policy Center, many people in lower-income brackets have negative tax rates or pay around 4-8% effective tax rate, and it's estimated that only 20-30% of taxpayers exceed Romney's 14% effective tax rate for income taxes alone.

journalist_explanation: Vote No On 2 said, "Amendment 2 will put almost 2,000 pot shops in Florida ... more pot shops than Walmart and Walgreens combined." The state health department did project 1,993 medical marijuana dispensaries would be needed to serve potential patients, based on data from Colorado compared with Florida. That is more than the 840 Walgreens and 233 Walmart supercenters and discount stores in the state, although the comparison seems like a bit of a red herring. It’s important to remember that while the health department report is the only real estimate available, this figure isn’t definite. The agency and the Legislature would decide the actual number of stores and how they are regulated after the amendment passes. That total is anyone’s guess. The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details. We rate it Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided states that a 2015 health department analysis estimated 1,993 registered treatment centers (dispensaries) in Florida, which is the same figure used by Vote No On 2 in their ad. United for Care, the group behind Amendment 2, does not dispute this estimate, and it is based on data from Colorado, which has a similar medical marijuana system.

journalist_explanation: A national advocacy group, in spotlighting Equal Pay Day, claimed that a pay gap between men and women exists in Oregon. PolitiFact Oregon has looked at the gap before and found that it’s real, but we took the next step by fact-checking the group’s claim that the gap is big enough to pay for 2,877 gallons of gasoline, 72 months of food or nearly 12 months of rent. All three elements of the claim checked out -- or were very close -- according to independent sources. We rate the claim True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided, including data from the U.S. Census Bureau and other reputable sources, supports the claim that women in Oregon are paid 79 cents for every dollar paid to men. Additionally, the calculations using actual gas prices, rent costs, and food plans demonstrate that eliminating the wage gap would enable a working woman in Oregon to afford approximately 2,877 gallons of gas (although slightly less than initially claimed), nearly 11.5 months of rent, and 72 weeks of food for her family, supporting the claim's validity.

journalist_explanation: When Riddle spoke, the U.S. misery index was 12.43 -- higher than the index over much of the previous 30 years. Riddle said, though, that the index was the highest it had been since Reagan succeeded Carter. That's not correct. The index was higher for nearly 30 months of Reagan’s presidency. His statement fails to account for the index’s full history. We rate his claim as False.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that the misery index in October 2011 (12.43) was not the highest since Ronald Reagan succeeded Jimmy Carter. According to the misery index site, the index was higher during a few months of Obama's term and was also higher in November 1990 under George H.W. Bush. However, it is noted that Reagan experienced higher misery indexes at the start of his presidency, specifically exceeding 14 for his first 25 months as president. Additionally, Riddle's campaign argued that changes in government methodology after 1980 may have affected the comparison.

journalist_explanation: Hannity said premiums are skyrocketing and the average man would pay twice as much, while the increase for the average woman would be 62 percent. That claim relies on a study that focused on the individual marketplaces for insurance set up under Obamacare, a subset of people who purchase insurance. Regardless of the accuracy of the analysis, it spoke to the experience of a small minority of Americans, and it did not factor in the subsidies that will cushion some people from increased premiums. Hannity overreached in his remarks on radio. That said, new rules for insurance plans will tend to push some rates up -- because the plans must provide better coverage. But by how much depends on a host of factors that several leading health policy experts say is too difficult to estimate. We rate this claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: While the Manhattan Institute study supports Hannity's claim that men are seeing their premiums double (going up 99 percent) and women's premiums going up by 62 percent, this conclusion only applies to people buying insurance through the marketplaces (the "individual market") and does not account for federal government subsidies that can reduce out-of-pocket expenses. Additionally, Kaiser Family Foundation expert Larry Levitt questions the validity of comparing costs before and after Obamacare due to changes in plan coverage and lack of reliable data on current premiums. Therefore, it cannot be determined with certainty whether Hannity's overall claim is true or false based on the evidence provided.

journalist_explanation: Providence City Council President Michael Solomon said, "Pregnant women who stand for five or six hours at a time increase their risk of pre-term pregnancy by 80 percent," attributing the statistic to the Women's Fund of Rhode Island. That's a very specific claim. But the evidence is based on a few studies, cherry-picked from a larger body of research that suggests that the risk, if there is one, is significantly smaller. Because the statement contains some element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression, we rate it Mostly False. (If you have a claim you’d like PolitiFact Rhode Island to check, email us at [emailprotected] And follow us on Twitter: @politifactri.
generated_explanation: The evidence provides conflicting information regarding the 80 percent increased risk of pre-term pregnancy associated with standing for five to six hours at a time. While some studies, such as those referenced by the Women's Fund and Council President Solomon, suggest an 80 percent increased risk, other studies published in reputable journals, including Obstetrics and Gynecology, suggest a significantly lower risk, ranging from 20-30 percent. Additionally, experts quoted in the article express varying opinions on the matter. Therefore, it cannot be determined with certainty whether the claim is true or false based on the evidence provided.

journalist_explanation: Sanders said that Clinton called Obama "naive" for saying he was would "sit down and talk to the Iranians" during the 2008 Democratic primary. This is a simplified description of the back-and-forth between Clinton and Obama. Both candidates said they supported more diplomacy between Iran and the United States than what the Bush administration had pursued. Clinton’s position differed from Obama’s in that she supported a slower approach, starting with lower-level talks. Obama, on the other hand, said he would be willing to meet with Iranian leaders in his first year as president, without preconditions. It was Obama’s approach to diplomacy with Iran that she called naive, not the idea of pursuing diplomatic relations in general. Ultimately, Obama did not meet himself with Iranian leaders in his first year. Sanders’ statement is partially accurate but takes things out of context, so we rate it Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that Hillary Clinton did call Barack Obama's position on talking to Iranian leaders "naive" during the 2008 Democratic primary, but not because she shut the door on diplomacy. Instead, she advocated for a more cautious approach than Obama, and was critical of his willingness to meet with Iranian leaders without preconditions in his first year as president. This nuance is misrepresented by Sen. Bernie Sanders when he claims that Clinton called Obama "naive" and that it turned out Obama was right.

journalist_explanation: Israel said: "When adjusted for inflation, per student spending has remained relatively flat over the past 16 years. Despite that trend, Texas schools in 2017 will receive $381 less per student than they did in 2003." Per-student funding has held relatively flat, data shows. But the "$381 less" conclusion rests on cherry-picking a timeframe and relying on an inflation index not favored by the main agency that advises lawmakers on budget issues. Try a different timeframe and/or the CPI and you can get contrary results--even, in some instances, greater spending in 2017. We rate this statement Half True. HALF TRUE – The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context.Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that there is disagreement between the Center for Public Policy Priorities and the Legislative Budget Board on how to adjust for inflation when comparing per-student spending. While the center's analysis using a federal inflation index (Implicit Price Deflator) suggests that per-student spending has remained relatively flat over the past 16 years and will be $381 less in 2017 than in 2003, the budget board's analysis using the Consumer Price Index indicates that per-student aid in 2017 will actually be up by $33 from 2003.

journalist_explanation: Romney was slightly off by saying 25 percent, but the actual number is 21.5 percent, so he was in the ballpark. We rate his statement Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The claim states that 500,000 federal workers make more than $100,000 a year, which is close to one-fourth of the federal workforce. However, evidence from the Office of Personnel Management shows that as of June (the most recent month available), there were 459,016 federal workers who made at least $100,000 in average base salary each year, accounting for 21.5% of government employees. This is a little short of the claimed 500,000 and one-fourth of the workforce, suggesting that the claim may be an overstatement or simplification of the data.

journalist_explanation: Taylor claimed "We saw the prison population expand and vacancy rates for correctional officers go from 2.9% to 15.2%" over the last eight years. The Legislative Audit Bureau said the adult inmate population has increased in the last eight years, from 21,941 in 2011 to 23,675 in 2018, or by 7.9%. And Corrections Department numbers show she is correct about the staffing vacancies as well. We rate the claim True.
generated_explanation: The claim is supported by evidence from the May 2019 report from the Legislative Audit Bureau and data from the Wisconsin Department of Corrections, which show that the prison population did indeed expand over the last eight years (growing 7.9% from 21,941 in 2011 to 23,675 in 2018), and vacancy rates for correctional officers increased significantly during this period, rising from 2.87% in 2011 to 15.27% in 2019.

journalist_explanation: Scott said that while Crist was governor, "utility costs went up 30 percent and went from below the national average to above the national average. Since I got elected, utility rates have come down 11 percent and now we are below the average." Scott is off in a lot of ways. First, his statistics don’t parse out the base rate from the rest of anelectric bill, which is critical to understanding how bills go up. Doing so shows base rates for the four large investor-owned power companies have consistently gone up under Scott’s watch. Perhaps more egregiously, Scott’s campaign fumbled the data in a report to make it seem like rates were much lower when Crist took office and higher when he left. We found the right numbers, and it paints a completely different picture. On comparing the state to the rest of the country, data shows Florida’s rates were higher than the national average well before Crist took office, but the gap narrowed during his time in office. Florida is now below the national average, but it’s not because prices dropped under Scott. By several measures overall rates are actually higher now than they were when he took office, despite a decrease in fuel costs. There’s so much incorrect in Scott’s statement. We rate it False.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided by the Public Service Commission and the U.S. Energy Information Administration, during Charlie Crist's administration, utility costs did increase, but only by 2.5 percent, not 30 percent. Additionally, while Florida was above the national average in residential utility rates when Crist came into office, it was already consistently higher than the rest of the country since October 2005. By the time Crist left office, Florida's rates were still higher than the national average, but by considerably less than when he came in. During Scott's tenure, Florida's rates have increased again, and while they are now below the national average, it is not because rates have decreased under his watch.

journalist_explanation: Bush said, "We have an 80 percent graduation rate in high school after spending more per student than any country in the world other than Liechtenstein, I think, or Luxembourg and a couple other small countries." The national average for the graduation rate was 81 percent in 2012-13, according to one method the federal government uses to calculate the rate. Among advanced countries, the United States ranked fifth in per student spending for secondary education behind Austria, Luxembourg, Norway and Switzerland. Liechtenstein wasn’t on the list, but since Bush expressed uncertainty, we think his statement is still accurate. We rate this claim True.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that while Jeb Bush's claim is true in terms of graduation rates, stating an 80 percent national average for high school graduation, it is disputed regarding his claim about per-student spending. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), four countries (Austria, Luxembourg, Norway, and Switzerland) spend more on secondary education than the United States. However, the OECD data does not include Liechtenstein, which Bush mentioned as one of the possible exceptions.

journalist_explanation: Scott said in a TV interview that "All Aboard Florida is a 100 percent private venture. There is no state money involved." While All Aboard Florida is a private venture, it has applied for a $1.6 billion federal loan. Also, the state is kicking in money for infrastructure, particularly for a new intermodal center at the Orlando International Airport. The funding for that infrastructure doesn’t go directly to All Aboard, but All Aboard does derive some benefit from the spending. Overall, we rate Scott’s claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: Although Scott stated that All Aboard Florida is a "100 percent private venture" with "no state money involved," evidence shows that federal dollars and state money are indeed associated with the project. Specifically, All Aboard has applied for a $1.6 billion federal loan, and there are plans to use state funding for quiet zones, intermodal transportation facilities at the Orlando International Airport, and connecting to Tri-Rail.

journalist_explanation: The claim here is that Mack "took seven and a half years to finish college."There’s a kernel of truth to that statement. Mack enrolled at Sante Fe Community College in 1986 and graduated from the University of Florida with a bachelor’s degree about seven and a half years later in 1993.But UF records show that Mack did not take classes for two of those years, 1991 and 1992. There’s also a minor point that Mack says he was dual-enrolled in community college at the same time he was completing his high school degree.Those, to us, are critical facts that would give someone seeing the ad a much different impression of Mack’s college career -- which fits our definition of Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence from the Palm Beach Post article and interviews with officials from Sante Fe College and the University of Florida show that Mack attended community college for 2.5 years and then transferred to the University of Florida, graduating in May 1993. This is a total of approximately 6.5 years, not 7.5 years as claimed by LeMieux's campaign.

journalist_explanation: Valdez said: "One in six Texans don’t have health care. We’re the most uninsured state in the U.S." One in six Texans in 2016 lacked health insurance, according to government surveys, and the state remained No. 1 for its share of residents without coverage. It’s an exaggeration to say that all uninsured people have no health care. We rate this claim Mostly True. MOSTLY TRUE – The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from multiple sources, including the Census Bureau (September 2017 report) and the Kaiser Family Foundation, confirms that in 2016, Texas had the nation's greatest share of residents without health insurance, with rates ranging from 15% to 17%. Additionally, a Gallup survey (May 2018) also shows that Texas had the highest rate of uninsured residents in 2017, at 22.5%, which further supports the claim made by Lupe Valdez.

journalist_explanation: O’Reilly said that Muslim nations did not "call out" the people who celebrated the 9/11 attacks. So far as we can tell, there was no official condemnation of people celebrating the 9/11 attacks. However, Muslim governments, and religious leaders, condemned the attacks themselves, as did many average Muslims. O’Reilly’s statement is accurate as far as it goes, but it leaves out important information that might lead someone to reach a different conclusion. That meets our definition of Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that there were no official condemnations of the people who celebrated the 9/11 attacks by Muslim nations, but it also shows that many governments and top religious leaders condemned the attacks themselves, which is a different statement. Additionally, average Muslims in some countries attended public events to voice sympathy for the victims and repudiate the attacks, indicating that not all Muslims supported the celebrations.

journalist_explanation: A Facebook post claimed that "89,000 children were separated from their parents under Obama" and "only 1,900 children have been separated under Trump." Immigration experts have told PolitiFact that family separations under Trump happened at a larger scale than they did under Obama. The Obama administration did not have a "zero-tolerance" policy that led to systematic family separations, as did Trump’s administration. A spokeswoman for Homeland Security previously told PolitiFact that the Obama administration did not track the number of families separated. The Facebook post’s 89,000 number might be a reference to a number of children placed with sponsors during Obama’s administration — but those children arrived alone without a parent or guardian. That doesn’t mean they were separated from their parents. The exact number of children separated under Trump is unclear, but based on previous data provided by Trump officials, the number at least surpasses 1,900. The Facebook post is inaccurate. We rate it False.
generated_explanation: The claim that 89,000 children were separated from their parents under Obama is disputed by immigration experts and the Department of Homeland Security, which states that the Obama administration did not count the number of families separated. Furthermore, a Senate subcommittee report explains that almost 90,000 unaccompanied immigrant children were placed with sponsors in the US between FY2014-2016, but notes that HHS places most of those children with their parents or legal guardians. This suggests that the 89,000 figure may actually refer to children who arrived at the border alone without a parent, rather than being separated from their parents as a result of policy. The claim about only 1,900 children being separated under Trump is also supported by evidence, but this does not change the fact that the initial claim about Obama's administration is likely false.

journalist_explanation: Watson said the average Austin homeowner pays about $1,300 to $1,400 just for recapture, as in funds ultimately spent in other districts. By the Austin district’s analysis, the owners of a home at the district’s average taxable value for 2016-17 stands to pay $1,355 in school property taxes toward the district’s more than $400 million recapture payment for the year. We rate this claim True. TRUE – The statement is accurate and there’s nothing significant missing. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided, including testimony from Nicole Conley and calculations from Jacob Barrett, supports the claim that in Austin, Texas, the average homeowner is paying about $1,300 to $1,400 just for recapture. According to Conley's prepared remarks, the Austin school district pays almost $2.6 billion in recapture payments to the state over five years, and Barrett explains how the district calculated the average homeowner's share of the budgeted recapture payment as $1,355. While one expert cautions that the "average" may not accurately describe the distribution of payment amounts, the evidence collectively supports the claim.

journalist_explanation: Crist said "some studies indicate" expanding Medicaid would "create about 120,000 jobs." Crist was referring to one study done for the Florida Hospital Association, a supporter of Medicaid expansion. That study predicted about 120,000 new jobs. There have been several studies that predict job growth related to Medicaid expansion, with one study putting the figure as low as 10,000 jobs. Crist cherry-picked the study with the highest statistic and omitted that it was done for an association that supports the expansion. Most economists and Medicaid experts say that it’s likely that the infusion of federal cash would lead to some jobs, but it is difficult to pinpoint the number. We rate this claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provides multiple studies with varying job growth predictions, including one study conducted by the Florida Hospital Association citing 120,000 jobs, and other studies from Moody's (10,000 to 30,000 jobs) and the White House Council of Economic Advisers (63,800 jobs). Experts interviewed by PolitiFact Florida also provided differing opinions on the job growth potential, making it difficult to determine a single accurate number.

journalist_explanation: Norquist said, "CBO reports that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate will reduce the deficit by $35 billion over 10 years." Norquist accurately reported the amount CBO estimated. However, his tweet cherry picks CBO’s conclusions, ignoring that the bill would produce 11 million additional uninsured Americans, and that the savings would amount to a one-time fiscal event. The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information, so we rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence confirms that the Congressional Budget Office reported that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate would reduce the deficit by $35 billion over ten years, as stated in their analysis released on September 6, 2013.

journalist_explanation: Greg Abbott said "Road congestion costs rush hour drivers in Austin and Dallas more than $1,000 a year. And in Houston, it’s even more -- almost $1,500 a year." Abbott’s claim was based on an annual Urban Mobility Report produced by the Texas Transportation Institute. While his figures match those in the report, critics have raised significant questions about how the numbers are calculated, as well as the premise that normal traffic conditions result in a congestion cost to motorists. They also point to the institute’s sponsors, most of which are transportation agencies that can be expected to use the report to advocate for additional funding for road projects. We rate this claim Mostly True. MOSTLY TRUE – The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the Texas A&M Transportation Institute's Urban Mobility Scorecard calculated the congestion cost for Houston to be $1,490 per commuter per year, which matches the claim made by Gov. Greg Abbott. Additionally, Tim Lomax, a senior research engineer at the institute, confirmed in an interview that this calculation includes both peak travel and off-peak travel times, and explained that the congestion cost cited by Abbott is not just for peak travel times as initially reported.

journalist_explanation: The Facebook post said that "in 1916, the U.S. government predicted that by the 1940s all paper would come from hemp and that no more trees would need to be cut down." The most plausible source for this -- Bulletin 404 -- is silent on this claim, and neither our own research nor any of the dozen experts we asked was able to come up with a definitive source. As with all claims of this type, it’s impossible to prove a negative, so we are willing to re-rate this claim if credible evidence emerges. However, our best efforts have turned up nothing more than a puff of smoke. Since the claim is unsupported, we rate it False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that multiple experts and sources within the United States Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Library, National Archives and Records Administration, and academia have searched for and found no reference to a prediction by the U.S. government that all paper would come from hemp by the 1940s. Bulletin 404, which is often cited as a source, does not make this claim and only discusses the technical feasibility of using hemp hurds to make paper.

journalist_explanation: Diaz-Balart said that in 2008, Obama had said that normalization with Cuba would first require "liberation of all political prisoners, and some basic steps toward freedom, including freedom of the press, political parties, labor unions." Obama did suggest such a linkage in 2008, though his phrasing was open to some interpretation. And on other occasions during the 2008 campaign, Obama offered a vaguer formulation for how Cuban relations could be normalized. On those other occasions, Obama said that if he saw unspecified steps toward democratic change in Cuba, he might pursue normalized relations with Cuba. Diaz-Balart’s claim glosses over these nuances, so we rate the claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: Diaz-Balart stated that during the 2008 campaign, Obama said that "before normalization would take place, there would have to be liberation of all political prisoners and some basic steps toward freedom, including freedom of the press, political parties, labor unions, etc." However, evidence provided shows that while Obama did make statements similar to this, he also stated in other instances that he was not prepared to immediately normalize relations with Cuba, but rather would move in that direction if there was progress on issues such as freeing political prisoners. Furthermore, an Obama spokesperson clarified that the president was "flexible on specifics" and willing to negotiate, indicating that his stance was more nuanced than a strict prerequisite for normalization.

journalist_explanation: A post claims, "If you have the Flu… get these two items… Sambucol [and] Oscillococcinum… in 48 hours you will feel better. In 72 hours you will be almost symptom-free." Overall, Sambucol has the most flu-fighting potential, but there is little evidence that Oscillococcinum can considerably shorten the length of the flu. And there isn’t enough evidence to prove that either of them can treat influenza better than antiviral medications. The post’s claim has an element of truth but leaves out critical context. We rate it Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The claim states that taking Sambucol and Oscillococcinum can cure flu symptoms within three days. While some studies suggest that Sambucol may have antiviral properties and be effective in treating influenza, the evidence is limited to small-scale trials with inconsistent results. In contrast, the effectiveness of Oscillococcinum remains uncertain due to biased studies and a lack of substantial scientific evidence. The claim's assertion that it can cure symptoms within 72 hours seems exaggerated based on the available research.

journalist_explanation: The blog post said that "over 73 percent of all donations raised (from the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge) are going to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations." Whether purposely or by incompetence, the anonymous blogger misreported the ALS Association’s figures. In reality, nearly 79 percent of the ALS Association’s expenditures were for purposes that advance its stated mission. Fundraising, overhead and executive salaries account for no more than 21 percent. We rate the claim Pants on Fire.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided, over 73% of donations raised by the ALS Association are not going towards fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations as stated in the claim. The correct breakdown of expenses is: Research: $7.2 million (27 percent), Patient and community services: $5.1 million (19 percent), Public and professional education: $8.5 million (32 percent), Fundraising: $3.6 million (14 percent), Administration: $1.9 million (7 percent). The claim specifically labels 73% of the group's spending as "fundraising, overhead, executive salaries and external donations", which is flat wrong according to the evidence.

journalist_explanation: Perry said that Obama called Medicaid "broken." In context, it’s clear the president was including Medicaid as a significant part of the entire health care system and that his larger point was that health care costs need to be reined in. Still, Obama described expanding the Medicare and Medicaid rolls as putting "more people in a broken system." We rate the governor’s statement as Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The claim states that Obama called Medicaid "broken" four years ago, which is not entirely accurate. According to the evidence provided, Obama did call the health-care system "broken" in 2009, but he specifically mentioned Medicare and rising healthcare costs as factors contributing to the problem. In his speech on June 2, 2009, he only mentioned putting more people into a broken system, without specifically referring to Medicaid. However, in a letter sent to Senate Democratic leaders after that meeting, Obama did mention Medicaid as one of the main drivers of budget deficits and soaring healthcare costs. Therefore, it can be argued that Perry's claim is partially true but not entirely accurate, as it takes out of context and misrepresents Obama's original statement.

journalist_explanation: Perry said he had "yet to get a response" to his 2010 letter to Obama requesting border security steps.That’s not so. Perry fielded a reply to his letter from a White House deputy about three weeks after the airport howdy. We grant that it might not have contained the answers Perry sought, but saying Perry has yet to get any response strikes us as both inaccurate and ridiculous. Pants on Fire!
generated_explanation: According to the provided evidence, John O. Brennan's letter of August 27, 2010, sent on behalf of President Obama, acknowledges Governor Perry's concerns and requests for border security assistance, indicating that the White House did respond to the governor's letter. This contradicts Governor Perry's claim that he has "yet to get a response" from Barack Obama.

journalist_explanation: Trump said President Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out of this country." Trump is referring to a 1954 campaign known as "Operation Wetback." While the idea that the operation resulted in more than 1 million deportations is not pulled out of thin air, historians widely cite that number as far too high for a variety of reasons -- including the fact that hundreds of thousands of undocumented immigrants would have had to self-deport. Also, it wasn’t just a deportation program. The campaign accompaniedmore legal immigration opportunities. We rate Trump’s claim Half True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, while President Dwight Eisenhower did oversee "Operation Wetback" which targeted illegal immigrants, the estimated number of people deported ranges from 250,000 to 1.3 million, not 1.5 million as claimed by Trump. Additionally, the operation's primary goal was to implement policy changes allowing more opportunities for immigrants to gain legal status through work visas, rather than solely focusing on deportation.

journalist_explanation: American Crossroads packs a bunch of claims into one sentence in its ad: "Sen. Nelson cast the deciding vote for Obamacare,cutting Medicare spending by $700 billion and letting an unelected board decide what gets covered here."Let’s summarize on the three points:• Nelson cast a vote in favor of the health care law, but news reports suggest he was not even one of a few final hold outs. He did not cast "the" deciding vote.• The health care law cuts future growth of Medicare spending by about $700 billion but it still grows. This part of the ad has some truth to it but requires further explanation.• The unelected IPAB board is tasked with finding Medicare savings. It can reduce how much government pays for services, and some fear that could lead doctors to not order certain treatments. It does not make decisions for individual patients, but it can recommend changes to bring down costs, including about what gets covered. Its powers are limited, however, and its decisions can be changed by Congress if Congress is willing to identify other savings. The Crossroads ad phrases its statements more carefully than some others we’ve seen, but it still gives a misleading impression about what the health care law means for Medicare beneficiaries. We rate this claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The claim states that Bill Nelson "cast the deciding vote for Obamacare cutting Medicare spending by $700 billion and letting an unelected board decide what gets covered here." However, according to the evidence, while Nelson did vote in favor of the bill on December 23, 2009, he was not one of the key votes that made the decision. The Los Angeles Times reported that Sen. Joe Lieberman, I-Conn.; Sen. Ben Nelson, D-Neb.; and Sen. Russ Feingold, D-Wis. were among those who held out until the last minute, but Nelson was neither an early activist nor a last-minute supporter of the bill. Additionally, the health care law's reduction in Medicare spending is not a cut, but rather an attempt to curtail future Medicare spending, and the Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) cannot ration care or deny treatments to patients.

journalist_explanation: Carson said "it’s not true" that his plan would leave us with a $1.1 trillion hole, as moderator Becky Quick said. But Quick’s math is sound, based on what's publicly known about Carson's plan. Carson’s 15 percent flat tax would generate a $1.1 trillion hole. By his own math, his plan would create a $1 trillion hole. We rate Carson’s claim False.
generated_explanation: The claim is from Ben Carson stating that his tax plan wouldn't leave the federal government with a $1.1 trillion hole. However, evidence shows that two different calculations were performed by CNBC moderator Becky Quick and Dr. Carson himself, resulting in conflicting conclusions. Quick's math suggests that Carson's plan would indeed fall short of anticipated revenue and spending by approximately $1.1 trillion, while Carson argued that his 15% tax rate on GDP would generate sufficient revenue to cover government expenses, claiming a smaller deficit. Given the differing calculations and explanations provided by both sides, it is not possible to definitively label the claim as true or false without further information or clarification on Carson's tax plan specifics.

journalist_explanation: Coulter said Fox News broke the story of George W. Bush’s 1976 drunk driving arrest. In terms of being the first to broadcast the story, that is correct. On the other hand, breaking a story has the strong meaning of having made the effort to uncover something that was obscure. In that sense, a local news station that happened to be a Fox affiliate gets the credit. While Fehlau's station was contracted to run Fox programming, it is independetly owned and not part of Fox News, the cable news channel. We rate Coulter’s statement Half True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided, Fox News did not break the story of George W. Bush's drunk driving arrest in 2000. Erin Fehlau, a reporter with the Portland Fox affiliate WPXT, first got wind of the arrest and began following the paper trail. Fox News then contacted Fehlau's news director to confirm the information, who in turn called Fox News in New York City, where they confirmed the story with Bush's campaign staffer. Fox News broadcast the story at 6 p.m., but it was WPXT that broke the story and conducted the investigation.

journalist_explanation: King, urging his readers to support an American assault weapons ban, said that since Australia passed tough gun laws, "homicides by firearm have declined almost 60 percent." The raw numbers back him up — but cause and effect are much peskier questions. Scholars we spoke with say the evidence leans King’s way, but is less than conclusive. That’s an important clarification. We rate King’s claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: According to Philip Alpers' statistics, the number of gun homicides fell from 69 in 1996 (excluding the 35 victims of the mass shooting prompting the laws) to 30 in 2012, which is a decrease of 56.5 percent. Additionally, Andrew Leigh and Christine Neill's study found that firearm homicides dropped 59 percent in the decade after the gun laws.

journalist_explanation: At two campaign rallies leading up to the election, Menendez claimed that under Obama, the United States has created "five million jobs."That’s only true if you’re talking about private-sector job growth since February 2010. When you factor in public-sector job losses and start counting at different points during Obama’s first year in office, the employment picture is far from what Menendez claimed.We rate the statement Half True. To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that the claim is true when considering the net increase of nearly 5 million private-sector jobs since February 2010, but false or less accurate when using different time frames and accounting for public sector job losses. Additionally, the article notes that experts believe presidents have limited impact on employment changes, suggesting a nuanced interpretation of Obama's role in job growth.

journalist_explanation: While the U-6 measurement is not the official gauge of unemployment in the United States, it’s a valid statistic to consider in conjunction with others. It's true that BLS describes it as a "labor underutilization" rate rather than an "unemployment" rate, since some of the people it counts are part-time workers who aren't officially "unemployed." While this distinction is important to PhD economists, we don't think it's a major problem for a speech made to the general public. In other words, for a general audience, we think "the real unemployment rate" is acceptable shorthand for "the labor underutilization rate," especially when a brief description of the measure is provided. So we rate this claim True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) offers a broader measure of labor underutilization known as "U-6", which takes into account not only the unemployed but also those marginally attached to the labor force and working part-time for economic reasons. According to the data, in January 2012, the U-6 rate was 15.1 percent, which supports Romney's claim that the real unemployment rate is over 15 percent if you take into account all the people who are struggling for work or have just stopped looking.

journalist_explanation: Trump said, "Four times, I said (McCain) is a hero but you know … people choose selective pieces." Trump literally said McCain is a hero five times, but never without caveats. Once, he added "perhaps, I believe" before conceding the point. Twice, he was interrupted. And the last two times, Trump said, "He is a war hero because he was captured." In other words, Trump also chose "selective pieces"and misquoted himself. We rate his claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, Donald Trump indeed stated that John McCain is "a war hero" five times during an interview on July 18, but he added caveats such as "because he was captured" and implied that being a prisoner of war isn't necessarily an achievement.

journalist_explanation: Sturtevant said that Virginia had zero percent economic growth last year, the third worst result in the nation. We rate his statement True.
generated_explanation: According to preliminary figures from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, Virginia's GDP experienced 0.0 percent inflation-adjusted growth in 2014, ranking it among the states with zero percent growth alongside Alaska and Mississippi, which actually saw a decrease in their state economies.

journalist_explanation: Michelle Malkin said former Republican Governor Pat McCrory "shepherded in driver’s licenses for illegal aliens in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks." For the most part, her claim isn’t supported by the facts. North Carolina hasn’t allowed unauthorized immigrants to get driver’s licenses since 2006, when a Democratic governor signed an act requiring driver’s license applicants to provide a valid Social Security Number. We found widely varying estimates on the number of people living in North Carolina illegally who are currently ineligible for driver’s licenses. Although North Carolina decided to allow DACA recipients to access driver’s licenses during McCrory’s tenure as governor, he said he followed that "reluctantly" and did not support making the larger population of immigrants living here illegally eligible for driver’s licenses. We rate the claim Mostly False. Editor's note: This item has been updated with comments from former Gov. Pat McCrory.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that Pat McCrory opposed allowing immigrants living in the country illegally to get drivers' licenses. Additionally, during his term, DACA recipients became eligible for driver's licenses, but these licenses included language indicating "Legal Presence" and "No Lawful Status," and the governor emphasized that he was following the law reluctantly. The claim that McCrory "shepherded in" driver's licenses for illegal aliens is therefore not supported by the evidence.

journalist_explanation: Cruz said the Obama administration spent "$205,075 in ‘stimulus’ to relocate a shrub that sells for $16." Some $130 million in stimulus money is supporting a $1 billion California road project that when it started brought to light a thought-to-be-extinct shrub in the wild. But we learned local road toll revenues covered the shrub’s $148,000 move and transplantation--not stimulus aid. Also, there’s a distinction between the rare in-the-wild version the shrub ballyhooed in the city by the bay and the occasionally available commercial versions, which this claim fails to acknowledge. We rate the statement, which has an element of truth but ignores critical facts such as the singularity of the shrub whose move wasn't funded from stimulus aid, as Mostly False. MOSTLY FALSE – The statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: According to multiple sources, including CNSNews.com and a CalTrans official, $205,075 was spent to relocate a shrub (Franciscan manzanita) from its original site. This amount includes costs such as digging up the shrub ($100,000), support services from experts ($35,000), and transferring funds for plant-related costs in a 15-year memorandum of agreement ($79,470). The claim that this money was spent on stimulus funds is also supported by reports showing grants funded by the economic stimulus package contributed to funding the road project.

journalist_explanation: Scott for Florida’s new ad about education costs said, "Charlie Crist allowed college tuition to increase up to 15 percent every year." Tuition did go up 15 percent in 2009 and 2010. But the ad downplays the fact that tuition increased 5 and 6 percent the two years prior to that. (It also neglects to mention it went up 15 percent under Gov. Scott one year, as well.) We should also note that Crist wasn’t the only actor here. The Legislature approved increases, as did the state Board of Governors. Still, tuition did go up each year, and as high as 15 percent for two years. We rate the statement Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while Crist allowed college tuition to increase up to 15 percent per year under a specific plan he advocated for in 2009, this was not a policy he initiated or supported from the start. In fact, he opposed raising tuition in 2007 and vetoed a 5 percent increase set by lawmakers at the time. The Legislature's own actions played a significant role in allowing tuition increases, and Crist did not have unilateral control over the process.

journalist_explanation: Perry talked about binational health insurance in a 2001 speech, as Santorum said. However, his dig about Perry's mention wrongly implies that the governor is working to establish binational health insurance. We found no evidence of Perry taking further action in the 10 years since. We rate Santorum's statement Half True. To comment on this ruling, "like" us on Facebook.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that in 2001, Rick Perry spoke at an August summit on border issues hosted by the University of Texas-Pan American. In his speech, Perry mentioned binational health insurance as a potential solution to address shared health care problems between the US and Mexico, specifically referring to a legislative proposal establishing a study on its feasibility. Additionally, an editorial on Perry's state website in 2001 highlighted the same bill that led to the 2003 report, which discussed binational health care coverage as a possibility for border residents.

journalist_explanation: Southerland said, "If you have a job in this country, (there's a) 97 percent chance that you're not going to be in poverty." That’s true only for full-time jobs. If you include both full-time jobs and part-time jobs, then the percentage drops slightly, to 93 percent. On balance, we rate his claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from the Census Bureau data in 2012 shows that 2.9% of Americans between 18 and 64 who worked full-time, year-round were in poverty, supporting Rep. Southerland's claim. While it is noted that a more accurate number for the likelihood of poverty "if you have a job" is around 93%, which is close to but slightly off from 97%, this does not contradict the overall truthfulness of the original statement.

journalist_explanation: Dolan said U.S. bishops have supported expanding health care since 1919. He’s correct that the National Catholic Welfare Council published pro-health-care expansion literature that year, and experts told us that the bishops have regularly supported proposals to expand health care over the years, despite disagreements over specific provisions enacted under Obama, including contraception regulations. We rate Dolan’s claim True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that in 1919, a group of US bishops published the Bishops' Program of Social Reconstruction, which included a section advocating for "comprehensive provision" of social insurance against illness, among other things. This historical document supports Cardinal Timothy Dolan's statement about the Catholic church's stance on health care dating back to 1919.

journalist_explanation: Clinton said, "One-half of undocumented workers pay federal income taxes, which means they are paying more federal income taxes than Donald Trump pays." While there is no official figure, experts estimate that about half of all undocumented workers pay federal income taxes, if not more. So in a year when Trump does not pay federal income taxes, which has been the case in the past, undocumented immigrants who do federal pay income taxes would pay more than him. But Clinton makes it seem as if this is a present state, and we don’t know anything about Trump’s current tax situation because he has not made his tax returns public. For that reason, we have no way of comparing Trump’s federal income tax payments to those of any given undocumented immigrant. We rate Clinton’s claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that a significant portion of undocumented immigrants pay federal income taxes through payroll taxes and ITINs. Estimates from experts at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center and the University of Texas suggest that around half of all undocumented workers pay federal income taxes, which is supported by data on Social Security payments and ITIN filers. In contrast, there is no clear evidence of Trump's current tax burden, as he has refused to release his tax returns, making it impossible to determine whether he pays more in federal income taxes than undocumented immigrants.

journalist_explanation: The Republican Party of Florida said Crist rode on a jet that "belongs to a serial polluter with a history of environmental violations fined nearly $2 million for polluting water." The plane’s owner, Bay County contractor James Finch, has been fined in the past for filling in wetlands or allowing unfiltered runoff to flow into waterways, in violation of environmental permits. That’s a legitimate definition of polluting, and there’s no doubt Finch has been fined almost $2 million over the years. It’s hypocritical of the state GOP to call out Finch when one of his subcontractors has benefited from a relationship with Gov. Scott. But that doesn’t change the facts. We rate the statement True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided by PolitiFact Florida's investigation, James Finch, the owner of the private jet used by Charlie Crist, has a history of environmental violations and was fined nearly $2 million for polluting water. The evidence cites specific instances where Finch's company, Phoenix Construction Services, was fined for environmental infractions, including backfilling a bayou at his home and improperly constructing the Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport.

journalist_explanation: Rothman claimed it costs more for the U.S. Mint to produce a penny and nickel than the face value of the coins.It costs 1.79 cents to produce and distribute every penny the Mint makes. And every nickel costs 9.22 cents.So, you can bank on those numbers. We rate the congressman’s statement True. To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: According to the U.S. Mint's most recent annual report cited in the evidence, it costs 1.79 cents to produce a penny and 9.22 cents to produce a nickel, which is more than their face value. This supports Rep. Steve Rothman's statement that it currently costs more than a penny for the U.S. Mint to make a one cent coin and more than a nickel to make the five cent piece.

journalist_explanation: Scott Arceneaux, executive director of the Florida Democratic Party, tried to discredit Scott’s influence on Florida’s economy on the eve of his State of the State address. Putting the blame for job losses squarely on Scott’s shoulders, Arceneaux said Scott cut "more jobs than he created in Florida in 2012."This claim is a bad case of cherry-picking. The Democrats honed in on the state’s bleakest period of job growth. Not only that, they held it up as a whole year’s performance.Yeah, 2012 was sluggish for job growth, especially compared to 2011. But it was an increase nonetheless.We rate the statement Pants on Fire!
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while Florida lost more government jobs (10,600) than private sector jobs were created (65,600) from December 2011 to December 2012, the overall nonfarm jobs total for 2012 showed a net gain of 54,900 jobs. This contradicts the claim that Gov. Rick Scott cut more government jobs than private sector jobs were created in Florida in 2012.

journalist_explanation: Casagrande said in a television interview, "Every American now is $51,000 in debt. That’s money I owe, that’s money my children owe before they even go to kindergarten, that’s their check to the federal government right now."A simple mathematical calculation confirms that every American technically owes the government $51,777.21 toward the national debt. But will youngsters have to suddenly start handing over their allowances to pay down the federal deficit? Not likely. We rate the statement Mostly True. To comment on this story, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the total national debt is indeed over $16 trillion, and dividing this number by the total U.S. population of approximately 314 million results in each person owing approximately $51,777. This calculation supports Assemblywoman Casagrande's claim that every American is $51,000 in debt.

journalist_explanation: Cruz says, "Existing law right now requires 700 miles of double-layered border fencing." He complains that Obama is ignoring the mandate. Such a law was passed in 2006 but no longer is on the books. It was amended in 2008, before Obama took office, and the double-layered fencing requirement was removed. About 650 miles of fencing now stands, of which 36 miles is double-layered. Cruz’s statement is long past its expiration date. We rate it False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that while existing law requires at least 700 miles of border fencing, it does not specify that this fencing must be double-layered. In fact, the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2008 amended the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to remove the requirement for double-layered fencing and instead mandate only a single layer of reinforced fencing.

journalist_explanation: Cornyn, Cuellar and Abbott said the federal government didn’t seek any 2017 flight hours to surveil the Texas-Mexico border via Operation Phalanx. Neither Cornyn or Cuellar provided factual documentation for this claim, which Cuellar otherwise attributed to a Texas official who didn’t respond to our inquiries. Separately when we asked, federal authorities didn’t document a specific request for 2017 surveillance hours. Regardless, the CBP commissioner’s letter to a Defense Department underling, sentbefore the Texans leveled their claim, endorsed continued flights over the border, even specifying priority sectors. We rate this claim Mostly False. MOSTLY FALSE – The statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check. CLARIFICATION, 4:41 p.m., Jan. 31, 2017: After we posted this fact check, Drew Brandewie of Cornyn’s office emailed to say Cuellar initiated the letter--a characterization echoed by Victoria Glynn, a Cuellar spokeswoman. We then amended our headline and story to make more clear the claim wasn’t Cornyn’s alone. These changes didn’t affect our ruling.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that despite initial claims by Texas officials, including Sen. John Cornyn and U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, that the Department of Homeland Security did not request any hours of aerial surveillance for the U.S.-Mexico border from the Department of Defense for 2017, subsequent letters and statements reveal that the Department of Homeland Security had in fact requested support from the Department of Defense. Specifically, a letter dated Nov. 14, 2016, from Kerlikowske, the Customs and Border Protection commissioner, to McKeon, an undersecretary at the Department of Defense, prioritized the allocation of rotary-wing assets for border security operations, indicating that DHS was seeking continued support from DoD for Operation Phalanx in 2017.

journalist_explanation: O’Rourke said: "I’m one of two members of Congress out of 535 that takes no corporate cash, no political action committee money." Unsaid: no candidate can take corporate cash; that’s illegal. Otherwise, we found, O’Rourke was one of at least five (not two) House incumbents to keep no PAC contributions in the run-up to the 2016 elections. He alsohasn’t accepted PAC aid into 2017 though he drew on about $297,000 in PAC donations in his House bids of 2012 and 2014--actions not recapped in his Dallas call for contributions. We rate this claim Half True. HALF TRUE – The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided, U.S. Rep. Beto O'Rourke's campaign received $110,721 in contributions from conduit PACs, which include ActBlue, JStreetPAC, and the New Democrat Coalition PAC, during the 2015-16 election cycle. This indicates that O'Rourke did accept PAC money, contrary to his claim of not taking any.

journalist_explanation: did not change. The city of Portland made national headlines last month by landing in a year-end report of government waste, as compiled by U.S. Sen. Tom Coburn, R-Okla. His "Wastebook 2010" lists some laugh-out-loud examples of federal largess: $2.5 million on a Census Bureau commercial too ironic to be understood? More than $200,000 to study why political candidates make vague statements? Nearly $500,000 to maintain a lavish office for former U.S. House Speaker Dennis Hastert? (We’re not vouching for the accuracy of any of those statements.)But we’re pretty sure that entry No. 100 -- out of 100 -- did not make anyone at the Portland Bureau of Transportation chuckle."Why have one bike sign when you can have two?" reads the final entry from Coburn’s report. "Oregon spent $900,000 in federal stimulus funds on a new bike signage project even though the city already has similar bike signs, which it plans to leave up. ‘The new signs — which include arrows, distance, and travel times to key destinations — have a slightly different design than existing ones,’ according to a local biking website."With the entry, Coburn posted photos of the old and new bike signs, as snapped by Jonathan Maus of bikeportland.org, also known as the "local biking website." The roadside signs in the photos are at two different locations and look a little different from each other.Coburn’s clear implication is that the city doubled up on redundant signage. Local talk radio host Victoria Taft picked up on his theme on her blog:"Portland spent nearly $1,000,000.00 in federal ’stimulus’ money to install ‘bike path’ signs where they already existed."With her blog, Taft includes a photo of a "sharrow" mark, a white sign marked on the pavement to indicate a bike boulevard.
