The implication here is that the "sharrows" are redundant.PolitiFact Oregon wanted to know: Did Portland spend money for signs when there were already perfectly good signs in place? We asked the city for clarification.In 2009, Portland received $900,000 from President Barack Obama’s "America Recovery and Reinvestment Act" -- the stimulus -- to improve bicycle signage.About $69,000 of that money went for 450 new "wayfinding" signs, the ones singled out by Coburn as wasteful. (These are green and white signs alongside the road telling riders the distance and estimated time to get to Lloyd Center or to the Eastbank Esplanade or myriad other destinations.) The $69,000 also paid for 1,180 new yellow "safety" signs marking crosswalks for pedestrians and cyclists. In any case, $69,000 is a pretty small portion of the overall grant.What about the rest of the money? About $480,000 of the $900,000 was spent on the "sharrow" pavement markings snapped by Taft. The city used the federal grant to paint 2,100 federally approved sharrows to mark 23 miles of new bike boulevards, and 30 miles of existing bike boulevards. The existing bike boulevards were stamped with smaller circles, and those are still there. The sharrows are larger, about 3 feet by 9 feet, and give a uniform look to all bike boulevards.(That leaves $351,000 unaccounted for. Where did that go? Well, said Dan Anderson, spokesman for the transportation bureau, there’s overhead, engineering costs, project management costs, contractor compliance costs, and pollution and erosion control costs. So many costs. But that’s another story.)What does that leave us with? The 1,180 new crosswalk signs were not mentioned in the musings of Taft or Coburn, so we can ignore those. In no case did any of the 450 signs duplicate existing roadside signs, so we can rule those out as well.That leaves Taft’s sharrows."Those pictures on my blog were of signs on the roads just laid down by those workers. Just feet away were existing painted signs on the streets," Taft wrote to PolitiFact."Bicyclists already use the roads on which these signs were painted. Signs already existed there and new ones were therefore redundant and, in my opinion, a waste of taxpayer money."The new sharrows did duplicate smaller bike boulevard markings in some locations, but not even close to all of them. The photo Taft snapped was on Northwest Johnson Street, where several sharrows are located next to older and smaller bike circles, some faded, some not. (They also are along Northwest 24th Avenue.) Now, we wouldn’t have a problem if Coburn and Taft had dinged the city for wasting federal money on bike markings. Or for spending too much on overhead costs. But the message from the two was that all of the $900,000 was spent on slightly different signs where other signs "already existed." And that’s inaccurate. We rule the claim False. Comment on this item.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided seems to indicate a correction, but the original claim is not directly contradicted. However, it states that the work done was installing signs where there already existed bikeway marks, implying that the original claim might be partially true or misleadingly stated, rather than outright false.

journalist_explanation: Pelosi said that Trump’s plan for child care would mean that "70 percent of the benefits go to the people making $100,000 a year." The one comprehensive study released so far by an independent group supports Pelosi’s claim. It’s possible that different studies -- or a substantive change to the Trump administration proposal as it works its way toward enactment -- could weaken the certainty of Pelosi’s analysis. Based on what we know now, though, we rate her statement True.
generated_explanation: According to the Tax Policy Center's study, which Pelosi's spokesman confirmed she was citing during her CNN interview, 70 percent of total tax benefits in Trump's child care proposal would go to families earning more than $100,000. The reason is that Trump's plan relies on tax deductions, which are worth more per dollar for higher-income families due to their higher marginal tax rates.

journalist_explanation: Cantor said states are spending more on Medicaid than on education. His statement is correct, although it should be noted that a substantial portion of the dollars states are spending on Medicaid come from the federal government.We rate Cantor’s statement True.
generated_explanation: The evidence presents conflicting information about whether states are spending more on Medicaid than they do on K-12 education. According to the NASBO report, when considering total funds including federal dollars, states spent 23.9% of their total budgets on Medicaid, while K-12 education accounted for 19.8%. However, when examining only general fund expenditures, public schools received an estimated $235 billion (34.7% of all general fund spending), with Medicaid falling to second place at $133 billion (19.6% of general fund outlays). This inconsistency in the numbers presented by Cantor and the NASBO report does not allow for a clear determination of whether the claim is true or false based on the provided evidence.

journalist_explanation: Shea-Porter said in December that in 2014 "Granite Staters who hold individual policies from Anthem… can indeed renew their policies and keep their doctors and hospitals." New Hampshire policyholders were always able to extend their current policies 12 months, thanks to the state’s early renewal option. Anthem will not extend canceled policies after its Dec. 16 deadline, despite the White House allowing extensions until October 2014. That means that Shea-Porter’s statement was accurate when she said it, though it no longer applies today, since the renewal deadline has passed. But individual policyholders did have a chance to keep their same network of hospitals and doctors next year. Not everyone may have done so, which means some people may be forced to see other doctors at different hospitals. In New Hampshire, at least, people were given that opportunity. We rate this statement True.
generated_explanation: The evidence supports the claim that Granite Staters who hold individual policies from Anthem can indeed renew their policies and keep their current doctors and hospitals in 2014. Specifically, Lisa Guertin, president of Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield in New Hampshire, stated in a release that the company had sent notices to individual policyholders to remind them of the option to renew an existing policy earlier than its anniversary date, which would allow them to keep their current doctors and hospitals. Additionally, it is noted that those who renewed their existing plans before the deadline would have access to the same network of providers for 12 more months.

journalist_explanation: U.S. Rep. David Cicilline said that "with the exception of the last year or maybe the last two years, we were at 100 percent" when it came to the amount Providence contributed to the city's pension fund during the eight years he was mayor.But those last two years were not the exception.During the first three years when Cicilline was in office for the full fiscal year, the city's contribution fell short of 100 percent, ranging from 86 to 96 percent.But in the last five years of his term, the contribution was either close to or at 100 percent.Cicilline, in his off-the-cuff statement, mixed up where the years with the lowest contribution fell. But he made it clear a few times that he was citing figures from memory, so we’ll give him some leeway and rule Mostly True.(Get updates from PolitiFactRI on Twitter. To comment or offer your ruling, visit us on our PolitiFact Rhode Island Facebook page.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while Cicilline is correct in stating that his administration made contributions at or near 100% during most years, he was asked a specific question about how many times his administration funded the pensions at 100%, and his office's response does not directly address this question. According to the Buck Consultants report, the contribution level exceeded 100% only once, in the 2007 fiscal year, and averaged 100% over the subsequent three years, but dipped below 100% in later years. Therefore, it cannot be determined for certain whether Cicilline's claim is true or false based on the evidence provided.

journalist_explanation: White said the council, which organized Texas Muslim Capitol Day in Austin, "was recently listed as one of 82 organizations designated as a terrorist group by the United Arab Emirates." So it was. However, her statement failed to note the U.S. government shortly disagreed with the council’s inclusion on the list, saying it doesn’t consider the council a terrorist group. For our part, too, we found no independent indicator the council merits identification as a terrorist organization. On balance, we rate this singling out of a seemingly flawed designation Half True. HALF TRUE – The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the UAE listed CAIR as one of 82 organizations designated as terrorist groups, but it also indicates that this listing was part of a broader effort by the UAE to define extremism more broadly than other countries. Additionally, the State Department and various experts have questioned the inclusion of certain groups on the list, including CAIR, suggesting that the designation may not be based on any actual evidence of terrorism or terrorist ties. The context provided suggests that the listing was likely driven by ideological differences rather than a genuine concern about terrorist activity.

journalist_explanation: Nelson tried to whack accusations about his lower tax bill for a family pasture with a claim that Mack takes tax breaks of his own in the form of "two homestead exemptions."Mack and his wife both serve in Congress, representing two different states on opposite coasts, and that’s clearly an unusual situation. They each own their own homes in their respective states.While it’s true Mack and his wife have two homestead exemptions between them, it is not accurate for Nelson to say Mack himself has two homestead exemptions. That would not be lawful, and Mack’s county property appraiser has vetted his case and determined it proper.We rate the statement Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence presents conflicting information about Connie Mack's homestead exemptions. On one hand, Senator Bill Nelson claimed during a debate that Mack takes two homestead exemptions, which is "directly contrary to Florida’s Constitution." However, later it is explained by Nelson's spokesman that what he meant was that Mack is part of a family unit with his wife Mary Bono Mack and they can only take one exemption. Additionally, the Lee County Property Appraiser Ken Wilkinson and Mack's campaign spokesmen argue that Mack is entitled to the homestead exemption for his condo in Fort Myers because his finances are not co-mingled with those of his wife. However, William D. Shepherd, general counsel for the Hillsborough County property appraiser's office, still disputes this, saying that they should only have one homestead exemption as a family unit.

journalist_explanation: A video by an anti-stadium group claims the Austin City Council is poised to give more than $1 billion to a private company and receive nothing in return. While the City Council could potentially provide incentives worth millions of dollars as part of the soccer stadium deal, the scary "$1 billion giveaway" language of the video simply doesn’t stand up to close scrutiny. The lengthy time frame invoked and the countless unknown events that could impact the deal make the math used in the video meaningless. Factor in that the video also doesn’t account for any return on the city’s investment, and it is clear that the contentions are off base — and ridiculous. We rate the claim Pants on Fire! PANTS ON FIRE – The statement is not accurate and makes a ridiculous claim. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the claim of a "$1 billion giveaway" is based on a flawed mathematical analysis by the anti-stadium group. Two professors who study publicly funded economic incentives have disputed this figure, calling it "crazy" and stating that it doesn't pass the sniff test. They argue that the time value of money means that dollars in the future are worth less than today, making the $1 billion estimate overly simplistic. Additionally, the potential benefits to the city, such as jobs and tourism, are not considered in the anti-stadium group's analysis.

journalist_explanation: Crist said that Scott cut education by over a billion dollars, meaning thousands of teachers "lost their jobs" and "class sizes went up." The kernel of truth to this claim is that the number of teachers did decline and the percentage of classes out of class-size compliance rose in 2011. But this is outweighed by a long list of omissions -- and it doesn’t reflect Scott’s complete tenure. The first problem is it glosses over the fact that the cut took place in 2011, and was later followed by increases. In addition, it is an overstatement to suggest that "thousands" of teachers lost their jobs due to the 2011 state budget cuts. Statewide data shows the number of teachers dropped by about 1,405, but that includes departures for any reason, not just layoffs. The percentage of class sizes out of compliance with the mandate increased by about 1 percentage point between Crist’s last budget and Scott’s first budget. However, there are multiple district and state factors that influence class size and the compliance rules have repeatedly changed in recent years. We rate this claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that while there was a $1.3 billion cut to public schools in 2011, and some teachers did lose their jobs due to layoffs, the number of teacher layoffs statewide is estimated to be around 1,405, which falls short of the "thousands" claimed by Charlie Crist's campaign. Additionally, student enrollment increased between the 2010-11 school year and the 2011-12 school year, making it likely that some districts struggled with class sizes due to other factors such as rapid enrollment growth or budget decisions unrelated to state funding. The data provided also shows a small increase in non-compliance with class size caps from 5.48% under Crist to 6.56% under Scott, but this was followed by a decrease and is not directly linked to the state budget cuts.

journalist_explanation: Hegar said 1 in 5 Texans did not have health insurance coverage before the pandemic, and now "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65 don’t have access to health care insurance." Hegar is right about how many Texans under 65 were previously uninsured. The number of Texans without access to health insurance during the pandemic is harder to pin down, but her "nearly 1 in 3" remark reflects the latest available estimates. We rate this claim True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that before the pandemic, about 1 in 5 Texans under 65 did not have access to health care coverage (19.9% uninsured rate). Additionally, the report from Families USA estimates that after the pandemic, about 29% of adults in Texas were uninsured (around 1 in 3), which aligns with Hegar's claim.

journalist_explanation: Democrat Gavin Newsom recently claimed his GOP opponent for governor John Cox "parroted" President Trump on the issue of family separations at the border. His statement, made right after a discussion of Cox’s policies, wrongly implies Cox supports separating immigrant families. Cox has repeatedly stated he opposes the policy. Cox and Trump have both said Congress should solve the issue, offering one parallel between the two. But even on this point, they’re not in lock-step. Trump has falsely blamed Democrats in Congress for forcing the separations, while Cox hasn’t made that specific charge. If anything, Cox has "parroted" one of Trump’s talking points about who should solve the problem. But he hasn’t backed Trump’s policy. Newsom’s statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. We rate it Mostly False. MOSTLY FALSE –The statement contains some element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that John Cox stated his opposition to separating families at the border in multiple instances, including a press conference and a TV interview. While Cox does agree with Trump that Congress must solve the issue of family separations, this is not equivalent to "parrot[ing] Trump — almost verbatim" as Newsom claimed. Furthermore, PolitiFact has noted that Trump's claims about Democrats in Congress forcing the family separation policy are false, which undermines Newsom's implication that Cox and Trump share the same viewpoint on this issue.

journalist_explanation: Williams said a car driving Wolfe "ran through the students, hit one of them." This is an exaggeration of what happened. A group of protesters blocked the path of Wolfe's vehicle during the Oct. 10 Missouri homecoming parade. At some point, Wolfe's vehicle made contact with Butler — but the incident didn't require Butler to receive medical attention, or even stop protesting. Police reviewed the incident and described it as "incidental contact." Williams' statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. We rate it Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from various sources, including police, witnesses, and video footage, indicates that the incident was an "incidental contact" and not intentional. Multiple people, including the driver of Wolfe's car and those present at the parade, described the contact as accidental, and there is no credible evidence to support the claim that a car drove through or hit students intentionally.

journalist_explanation: Ryan said that six studies verify that the numbers in the Romney tax plan add up. Hearing that, you might think that each is independent research. But not all studies are created equal and these come from people or groups with ties to Romney.Two of those studies come from Feldstein, a Romney campaign adviser. Three come from conservative think tanks, the Heritage Foundation and American Enterprise Institute, which have analysts who advise the Romney campaign. While every analyst would insist that they make their own judgments, the Tax Policy Center is fully independent of the Obama campaign.The studies from Feldstein and Rosen use 2009 data. That was an abnormal year and one that made it easier to make the math work for the Romney plan. The analysts could have chosen other years but decided not to.Of the studies that examine the middle class tax burden, none shows conclusively that households making less than $200,000 would be spared a tax increase. That is a group of taxpayers that Romney defines as middle class and says he would protect.None of the studies can accurately model Romney’s tax plan because he has said so little about how he would pay for it. As a result, all of them make assumptions as to what tax breaks might be reduced. They can speak in rough terms about a concept, but they can not verify a plan when no detailed plan exists.We see no more than one fully independent study out of the six claimed. We rate the statement Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that several studies have varying estimates on whether the math adds up for Mitt Romney's tax plan, with some studies supporting it and others challenging its feasibility. However, none of the studies explicitly state that six studies verify that the math adds up. Additionally, two of the studies mentioned as part of the claim are editorials from The Wall Street Journal, which were previously counted in a previous claim of five studies and have since been dropped by the campaign.

journalist_explanation: In his tweet, Boehner said that Obama’s health care law is "expected to destroy 2.3 million jobs." Boehner’s use of the word "destroy" mischaracterizes what is going on, since the reduction will come from voluntary actions by workers, rather than layoffs by employers. The law would not push up unemployment. In fact, some people at the lowend of the wage ladder would find it easier to find work as a result of the predicted shifts in the workforce. In addition, it’s misleading to refer to 2.3 million "jobs," since CBO combined all incremental losses of hours worked into full-time-job equivalents. Under this scenario, we would expect many more than 2.3 million people to be affected, but many of them would cut their hours a few at a time, rather than quitting their jobs entirely. It can be easy to miss the distinction between jobs and workers -- and the CBO report is not all rosy for the nation’s economic future. But Boehner’s statement remains flawed. We rate the claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The CBO report estimates that workers will choose to work fewer hours, resulting in a decline of 2.0-2.5 million full-time equivalent workers by 2024. However, this does not translate to job losses due to employers cutting positions or layoffs; rather it's primarily voluntary choices made by workers who have access to less expensive health insurance options.

journalist_explanation: The general unemployment rate in June 2012 would have been 10.9 percent if the labor force participation rate had remained at the 65.5 percent in place when Obama became president. That’s about 11 percent.We rate Ryan’s statement True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that if the labor force participation rate were the same as when Barack Obama became president, the unemployment rate would be around 10.9-11.2 percent according to Cheryl Abbott's calculation using BLS figures and assuming all 4.6 million added workers are unemployed, not 11 percent as claimed by Paul Ryan.

journalist_explanation: One of PolitiFact’s Truth-O-Meter principles is that words matter, and at the very least, Smith's claim is worded ambiguously. The ERCOT analysis and a news release point to an increase in energy costs of 16 percent by 2030. Smith claims that increase per year. We rate this claim as False. FALSE – The statement is not accurate. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check. EDITOR’S NOTE 3:30 p.m., 12/18/15: After publication, Trip Doggett, ERCOT president and chief executive officer, emailed a statement saying Smith’s statement of 16 percent per year was based an erroneous information provided by ERCOT. "Because ERCOT inadvertently provided incorrect information to the Chairman’s staff, I would like to take this opportunity to state the correct information and offer an apology." This additional information did not change the rating of our claim.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that ERCOT estimated energy costs will rise as much as 16 percent by 2030 due to the EPA Clean Power Plan, but this increase is over a period of time from 2022 to 2030, not every year. If energy costs rose 16 percent each year until 2030, it would be roughly a 327 percent increase in the cost of energy, which contradicts the claim made by Rep. Smith that energy costs will rise as much as 16 percent per year.

journalist_explanation: Cruz said: "Every year we spend roughly $500 billion on tax compliance. That is roughly the budget of our entire military, entirely wasted on tax compliance." This claim proved squishy at both ends. It looks like depending on how you value time, you can get to almost any total for what it costs Americans to prepare and file tax returns. However, most estimates run short of Cruz’s figure. Meantime, military spending exceeded $800 billion when he spoke though the senator’s spokesman indicated he meant to not count spending on conflicts abroad and other items not in the military’s nearly $500 billion base budget. We rate the statement False. FALSE – The statement is not accurate. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that Cruz's claim of $500 billion spent on tax compliance is exaggerated. Multiple studies cited in the evidence, including those from the Laffer study and the Mercatus Center study, provide varying estimates of tax compliance costs, ranging from $67 billion to $378 billion a year. However, none of these studies support the $500 billion figure. The IRS's Taxpayer Advocate Service also estimated that individuals and businesses spent 6.1 billion hours complying with tax filing requirements, which would translate to around $192.6 billion in labor costs, not $500 billion.

journalist_explanation: Huber claimed that she’s never said "don’t build" Texas 45 Southwest.As far as we can tell, there’s no instance of Huber being so blunt. But her efforts to get the road pulled from the CAMPO plan and her stated desire not to proceed to construction without more information are evidence she doesn’t want the project built yet.These important details are not reflected in her statement, which we rate Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that Karen Huber has consistently expressed concerns about building Texas 45 Southwest without first proving its cost-benefit analysis, and has taken actions to remove it from the county plans and CAMPO plan. While she does not directly say "don't build it", her words "Prove the cost-benefit is there" and "I do not believe we should move forward with it till we conclude that it is going to do what they say it is going to do" indicate that she is opposed to proceeding with the project without further analysis.

journalist_explanation: Will said Reagan created 1 million jobs in one month. The reality is that the jobs createdby Reagan in 1983 were the result of a counting anomaly that started with astrike of telephone workers. The federal Bureau of Labor Statistics rightly discounted the spike when it first reported it in 1983, as did news reports. Will should have, too. We rate the claim Pants on Fire.
generated_explanation: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' employer data, the 1.1 million increase in paychecks in September 1983 was due to telephone workers returning to their jobs after a strike, which artificially inflated the job numbers for that month. The government's own report explicitly tied the spike to the labor dispute, and historians have confirmed that the strike accounted for most of the increase.

journalist_explanation: Goodlatte said enforcement of laws against lying on federal background checks for gun purchases "is down 40 percent" under Obama. The congressman had the percentage right, but he glossed over the law’s history of lax enforcement. During the Bush and Obama administrations, only a tiny fraction of 1 percent of the violations was prosecuted. The Justice Department has seen little value in prosecuting cases in which background checks have already stopped prohibited people from buying guns. Goodlatte, in seeking to level partisan blame, offered a juicy statistic without context. We rate his statement Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided suggests that there has been a decline in average annual prosecutions between the Bush and Obama years, with a 42 percent decrease. However, Goodlatte's claim of a 40 percent overall decline is based on incomplete data (only two years of statistics are available for Obama's administration), whereas Gutierrez counters by saying that both administrations have the "same dismal record." The article also provides additional context that explains why the Justice Department may not prioritize prosecutions in these cases, further complicating the issue. Therefore, it cannot be determined with certainty whether Goodlatte's claim is true or false based on the provided evidence.

journalist_explanation: Gingrich is right about the absolute number of Americans in poverty. A better understanding of the extent of poverty in the United States requires looking at the number of people in poverty as a percentage of the population. Measuring it that way, the current poverty rate is not the highest ever. Still, this rate is the second highest in more than four decades, which fits with Gingrich’s general point. However, we think Gingrich overstates the amount of blame Obama personally deserves for this statistic. On balance, we rate his statement Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence from the U.S. Census Bureau shows that the absolute number of people in poverty in 2010 (46.1 million) was at its highest since the statistic has been recorded, and Gingrich's statement is confirmed by this data. However, it also mentions that the poverty rate is not necessarily the highest when considering population growth.

journalist_explanation: Clinton said, "I spent 18 months putting together the sanctions against Iran so that we could force them to the negotiating table." Clinton’s claim is for the most part accurate, though a little exaggerated. During her first 18 months as secretary, the State Department was at the helm of a global effort to increase sanctions on Iran, culminating in an important U.N. resolution. Clinton was personally involved in these diplomatic efforts and pushed them publicly. And experts said these sanctions, on top of other sanctions passed before and after, were crucial to getting Iran to the negotiating table. However, Clinton wasn’t singularly responsible for the sanctions, just as the sanctions passed under her watch likely weren’t singularly responsible for opening up Iran to talks. We rate her statement Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that during her first 18 months as Secretary of State (January 2009 to June 2010), Hillary Clinton played a major role in increasing sanctions against Iran through diplomatic efforts and lobbying other countries, which was instrumental in getting the UN Security Council to approve tough new sanctions on Iran. Additionally, experts such as Patrick Clawson, Suzanne Maloney, and Richard Nephew confirm that Clinton's efforts were significant in contributing to the international sanction ramp-up against Iran.

journalist_explanation: The meme said police in the United States use tear gas even though it "has been classified as a chemical weapon and banned in international conflict since 1993." The Chemical Weapons Convention did outlaw the use of tear gas in warfare, though that went into effect in 1997, not 1993. However, the meme glosses over some context. It tries to leverage the Chemical Weapons Convention’s decision to ban tear gas as evidence of why the technique should be illegal for policing, yet that very same convention explicitly allows its use for domestic lawenforcement purposes. The claim is accurate but needs clarification, so we rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The claim that tear gas has been classified as a chemical weapon and banned in international conflict since 1993 is incorrect, as it is only banned for use in warfare under the Chemical Weapons Convention. Article II (9) (d) of the convention specifically states that law enforcement including domestic riot control purposes are permitted, not prohibited.

journalist_explanation: Beyer said "over 97 percent of the scientific community" believe humans are contributing to climate change. The studies Beyer and others cite do not reflect the scientific community at large. They are surveys that focus on the conclusions of climatologists, earth scientists and meteorologists. The studies found that overwhelming majorities of these experts - sometimes, but not always as high as 97 percent - say humans are contributing to global warming. Beyer’s statement is credible but needs elaboration. We rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The claim is supported by multiple studies and sources cited by NASA, including a study by John Cook in 2013, which found that 97.1% of abstracts and 97.2% of authors agreed with the consensus position on human-caused global warming. Additionally, other studies such as those from the University of Illinois (2009) and the National Academy of Sciences (2010) also support the claim, showing a high level of agreement among climate scientists that humans are contributing to climate change.

journalist_explanation: Trump claims that the CIA told the Bush administration that a domestic terror attack was coming. The report assembled over a span of three years after Sept. 11, 2001, found no specific alert. The potential for a domestic attack was discussed in early August, but it was mentioned only in broad terms and was not brought back up. Investigative reports in the years since found that the CIA warnings emphasized possible targets overseas. Tenet told investigators that as late as Sept. 10 he did not talk about a domestic attack with the president. There’s no support that Bush and top White House officials had, as Trump said, "advanced notice" of an attack on New York City or any other place in America. We rate this claim False.
generated_explanation: The commission report states that George Tenet told staff that "the system was blinking red" and that there were several threat reports, but none suggested a specific target on U.S. soil. Additionally, the August 6 briefing document titled "Bin Ladin Determined to Strike in US" noted unconfirmed warnings of possible attacks, but this was deemed historical by President Bush and did not lead to any meetings or actionable intelligence about an imminent domestic attack.

journalist_explanation: Clinton said Trump was one of the people who rooted for the housing crisis. While Trump did not welcome the tragedy of foreclosures for millions of Americans, he did speak optimistically about the opportunities the overall situation created for an investor such as himself. Clinton’s statement leaves out that nuance, but in large measure, it matches Trump’s words. We rate this claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that Donald Trump did express views similar to those quoted by Hillary Clinton, specifically in 2006 and 2007, where he hoped a real estate bubble would burst so he could buy properties at discounted prices. However, the same evidence also suggests that Trump was offering sound business guidance during these times, particularly when looking back on his statements from before the housing crisis collapsed. Additionally, in later interviews, such as with CNN in 2009, Trump framed the economic situation as a "great opportunity" to buy properties, but this time acknowledging the existing economic catastrophe caused by the housing crisis. This conflicting information makes it difficult to determine whether Clinton's claim that Trump rooted for the housing crisis is entirely true or false based solely on the provided evidence.

journalist_explanation: Sen. Corker says it has been more than three years since Congress passed a budget and that this year, not a single appropriations bill has made it the Senate floor. The record shows that he has his facts straight.While other Republicans have tried to lay the blame for the lack of a budget at the feet of Democrats, Corker does not specifically apportion blame just one party. He simply chastised the Senate in general for failing to pass a budget and we rate his statement as True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that while it is true that the last budget resolution was passed on April 29, 2009, there have been appropriations bills considered and approved by the House and Senate Appropriations Committee. However, none of these bills were brought to the Senate floor for a vote due to an ongoing dispute between the parties over spending levels. Therefore, Corker's claim that "not a single appropriations bill has been brought to the floor this year" is false because while no appropriations bills were voted on, they were considered and approved by committees.

journalist_explanation: Young’s ad says he voted against the controversial $716 billion Medicare cut.What he voted against was the Affordable Care Act, which implements an estimated $716 billion reduction in payments to hospitals and private insurers in effort to reduce the program’s ever-increasing costs. He could not have known the amount would be $716 billion, as that estimate came two years after the health care vote. Meanwhile, the Republicans have their own plan for reducing future Medicare spending, by bring more private insurance companies into Medicare and offering voucher-like premium support.The claim excludes several points. We rate it Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that the claim "Young opposed $716 billion cut to Medicare" is misleading. According to the Congressional Budget Office, the health care law did reduce Medicare outlays by $716 billion between 2013 and 2022. However, it's unclear if Rep. Young specifically knew he was voting against this particular aspect of the law at the time of the vote in 2010. Additionally, as pointed out in the evidence, Rep. Ryan's budget, which Young voted for twice, also assumes the $716 billion savings in Medicare spending. This conflicting information makes it difficult to determine with certainty whether the claim is true or false.

journalist_explanation: LaPierre wrote that "the president flagrantly defies the 2006 federal law ordering the construction of a secure border fence along the entire Mexican border."First, he misrepresented what the law required, which was segments of fencing in specific places, not a continuous fence along the 2,000 mile border. Second, he ignored the 2007 amendment which gave the government some discretion over how to build the fence.The fence that has been built -- just one mile short of what’s required -- is a combination of pedestrian fencing and vehicle barriers. To some critics that does not satisfy what Congress intended in 2006, and very little of it is double-layered. On that point, we think LaPierre’s statement contains a grain of truth.Otherwise, though, it’s clear that Obama is not flagrantly defying the law, especially as resources toward other aspects of border enforcement are increasing.We rate LaPierre’s statement Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The claim states that President Obama is flagrantly defying the 2006 federal law ordering the construction of a secure border fence along the entire Mexican border. However, the evidence shows that the Secure Fence Act of 2006 only required the construction of "at least two layers of reinforced fencing" in specific segments of the border, not along the entire border. Additionally, an amendment to the law in 2007 gave the Department of Homeland Security discretion to decide what type of fence was appropriate in different areas, and the fence constructed so far is mostly vehicle barriers or pedestrian fences that are not double-layered as specified in the original law.

journalist_explanation: Kerpen, among others, tweeted, "Amazing fact: Senate has already voted on more amendments in 2015 than (Harry) Reid allowed ALL YEAR last year." On the numbers, that is right. But experts cautioned us that the claim falls more in the interesting factoid category than a sign of a different or more cooperative Senate leadership. The statement is accurate but needs clarification and additional information. That meets our definition of Mostly True. Correction: An earlier version of this fact-check incorrectly described Sen. David Vitter's amendment.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that as of January 22, 2015, there were indeed more roll call votes on amendments in the Senate under new Majority Leader Mitch McConnell than there were in all of 2014 under former Majority Leader Harry Reid. This is confirmed by a search of Senate roll call votes on amendments in both years, which reveals a total of 15 votes in 2014 and 16 votes in 2015 up to that point.

journalist_explanation: Cornyn said, "Texas remains one of the most severely impacted states from drug trafficking. Nearly 3,000 Texans died from drug related deaths in 2017 – with half being overdoses involving opioids." Cornyn’s tweet as-written includes accurate figures about drug overdose deaths in Texas and across the country, but his characterization of Texas as one of the "most severely impacted states from drug trafficking" based on these deaths doesn’t take population into account. Looking at raw figures, Texas was among the states with the most drug-related deaths in 2017. But when we look at the rate of drug-related deaths (which accounts for population), Texas is at the lower end and had fewer drug overdose deaths per capita than 46 other states in 2017. Also: Cornyn’s tweet originated from comments he made at a Senate hearing, which suggested that he was looking at a range of factors when considering the severity of the impact of drug trafficking in Texas, not just drug overdose deaths. We rate this claim Half True. HALF TRUE – The statement is partially accurate but leaves out important details or takes things out of context.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there were indeed 2,989 drug-related deaths in Texas in 2017, with nearly half of those being overdoses involving opioids. This supports Cornyn's claim that "nearly 3,000 Texans died from drug related deaths in 2017 – with half being overdoses involving opioids." However, it is worth noting that the claim that Texas remains one of the most severely impacted states from drug trafficking may be misleading when considering population size.

journalist_explanation: Perry told reporters that France "wouldn’t buy Texas beef for some reason, yet 76 percent of their energy comes from nuclear power." Perry's main point holds up;France gets about three-quarters of its electricity from nuclear power. But his beefmention lacks clarification in that itwas the European Union (not France alone) that banned only hormone-raised beef. Some beef continues to be imported to the EU. We rate this claim Mostly True. MOSTLY TRUE – The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the EU has banned imports of beef produced with growth hormones since 1989, which explains why France wouldn't buy Texas beef. Additionally, official statistics from the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Paris-based International Energy Agency confirm that France relies on nuclear power for a significant percentage of its energy production, specifically stating that in 2016 it drew 72% of its electricity from 58 nuclear power plants, which is close to the claimed 76%.

journalist_explanation: Jindal said that in supporting an employer health insurance mandate in 1993, Clinton opposed an individual mandate. We think readers would be wise to review the red flags we raised surrounding Jindal’s characterization of Clinton’s comments and how they apply to the current state of affairs. But when it comes to reciting history, Jindal is largely accurate. Clinton had serious misgivings about an individual mandate to buy health insurance, and strongly preferred an employer-based model. On that point, we give Jindal a Mostly True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, in 1993 Hillary Clinton led a task force created by President Bill Clinton to reform the health industry and provide care for most of the population. She testified on the Hill for several days to explain and defend the plan before congressional committees. During her testimony, she stated that the administration settled on an employer mandate, rather than instituting a broad-based tax similar to Medicare or an individual mandate, as proposed by some Republicans.

journalist_explanation: Posts about a Christian pastor in Vermont being sentenced to one year in prison after refusing to marry a gay couple have circulated on the Internet. However, the article was published at a known fake-news site, and we found no evidence to support the existence of key elements of the story, including the pastor, church, or the judge referenced in the article. We rate this claim Pants On Fire.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the website publishing the article, NewsExaminer, is a fake-news site classified as such by Snopes. Furthermore, it was discovered that the Christian pastor mentioned in the article, Paul Horner, is a recurring name used in stories published by other fake news sites, and does not appear to be real. Additionally, the judge mentioned in the article, Hon. Myron Danus, does not exist as verified through various court administration offices.

journalist_explanation: The Tea Party blames Obama for an additional half million blacks being unemployed since he took office. The group’s number of 540,000 unemployed is correct, and the NAACP concurs that blacks are among Obama’s biggest supporters. We heard varying opinions on whether the president is to blame for that job loss and it’s clear there are a variety of factors at work -- some under the president’s jurisdiction, some not. Partially accurate claims that leave out important details fits the definition of our ruling: Half True. To comment on this story, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence from PolitiFact New Jersey confirms that a net of 540,000 additional black Americans did lose their jobs since Obama took office, as reported by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics in Washington, DC.

journalist_explanation: Abbott said, "I’ve sued the Obama administration now 25 times." Since Obama became president, Texas has filed or been a party to 27 lawsuits against the federal government. This statement is True.
generated_explanation: The claim that Greg Abbott has sued the Obama administration 25 times is conflicting because while the evidence shows that Texas has filed 27 lawsuits against the federal government during Obama's tenure, not all of these lawsuits are necessarily considered "suits" by Abbott himself. According to the article, some of these cases were initiated at the request of state agencies and were bundled together with other states' lawsuits. However, experts cited in the article argue that this does not necessarily mean Texas was not a real litigant. Additionally, some critics object to counting certain cases, such as those involving preclearance under the Voting Rights Act, as suits against the federal government.

journalist_explanation: Kasich said, "When I left Washington, we had a $5 trillion surplus." His rationale for the $5 trillion figure is reasonably sound, but he was inaccurate in how he referred to it. It was a 10-year cumulative projection for future surpluses, rather than a one-year actual surplus, and the savings turned out to be ephemeral due to unforeseen events. We rate the claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that while the Clinton administration projected a cumulative $5 trillion surplus over 10 years (2001-2010), there was no actual $5 trillion surplus when Kasich left Washington in 2000. Additionally, the projected surplus was not based on current funds but rather future projections subject to assumptions about growth in spending and revenues.

journalist_explanation: Greitens said the Democratic Governors Association and "the Obama political machine" spent $1 million against him leading up to the primary election. A PAC with the same address as the Democratic Governors Association made four in-kind contributions totaling that amount in the weeks leading up to the election. And though both Obama and the PAC hired the same company to work on their ads, there's no evidence to support Greiten's statement that the "Obama political machine" colluded with the PAC. We rate this claim as Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The claim that Democrats spent $1 million against Eric Greitens in the last couple of days is partially true, but only because a political action committee (Jobs and Opportunity) affiliated with the Democratic Governors Association made an in-kind contribution of over $1 million to Greitens' opponent Chris Koster's campaign. However, this contribution was reported as a series of smaller in-kind contributions totaling over $1 million, made beginning two weeks before the primary election. Additionally, there is no evidence that President Obama's political machine directly involved itself in the ad buy. While Greitens' campaign did issue a press release accusing Koster and Democrats of attempting to steal the election through "meddling," this appears to be an exaggeration or mischaracterization of the situation.

journalist_explanation: In a campaign mailer, Republican congressional candidate George Flinn blamed Steve Cohen for the unemployment rate in Shelby County being more than twice as bad now (4.8 percent to 9.7 percent) than it was in 2007 when he took office.But Flinn’s numbers are off, no matter if you stop the clock at the July numbers or the more recent September numbers. Further, the campaign overreaches by trying to pin responsibility for Shelby County’s economic collapse and then gradual recovery on one elected official. We rule this claim False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that the unemployment rate in Shelby County was actually 5.5 or 5.7 percent when Congressman Cohen took office in January 2007, significantly higher than the claimed 4.8 percent. Additionally, the current unemployment rate has been decreasing and was reported as 8.4 percent on October 25, contradicting the claim that it reached 9.7 percent.

journalist_explanation: Cruz said, "We have the lowest percentage of Americans working today of any year since 1977." He’s put his finger on a trend that worries economists of all stripes, but his wording was sloppy. In addition, it’s worth remembering that this particular trend is being driven at least to a degree by demographic trends beyond the control of any president. We rate the claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided indicates that Sen. Ted Cruz's statement is partially correct when considering the civilian labor force participation rate, which is at its lowest level since the 1970s. However, it also mentions an alternative statistic, the employment-population ratio, for which Cruz's claim is incorrect as it has been improving in recent years and was not at its current rate in 1977 according to that measurement.

journalist_explanation: Congressman Holt claimed that as a potion of the nation’s economy, government support for research and development has "fallen by nearly two-thirds since the 1960s."Data on federal expenditures from the National Science Foundation show that as a percentage of the gross domestic product, spending has dropped by 62 percent since 1964.We rate his statement True. To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that according to the National Science Foundation data, federal expenditures for research and development peaked in 1964 at 1.92% of GDP and decreased to .73% by 2008, which is a decrease of 62 percent or nearly two-thirds. This supports the claim made by Rep. Rush Holt.

journalist_explanation: Slaughter said that "by 4th grade, 86 percent of African-American boys and 82 percent (of) Hispanic boys are reading below proficiency level." Government data backs up that depressing statistic, though it’s worth noting that the U.S. has at least seen improvements across all races since the early 1990s. We rate the statement True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that the Nation's Report Card states that 14% of black boys and 18% of Hispanic boys read at a proficient level, which means that 86% of black boys and 82% of Hispanic boys are not proficient. This contradicts Slaughter's claim that 86% of African-American boys and 82% (of) Hispanic boys are reading below proficiency levels by the fourth grade.

journalist_explanation: Rowden said Webber "voted to allow sex offenders to be within 500 feet of childcare centers and playgrounds, and even voted to allow sex offenders to be coaches." That’s a misleading version of events. Webber actually supported the House version of the legislation in question. But the bill was amended in the Senate to include a provision that allowed some sexual offenders to have their names removed from the sexual offender registry. Webber opposed that addition, his campaign said, and voted against the final bill. There is an element of truth to this claim but not much more. We rate it Mostly False.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, Stephen Webber initially voted in favor of Missouri House Bill 62, which banned sex offenders from being within 500 feet of childcare centers and playgrounds, and from coaching children. He then changed his vote after the bill was amended by the Senate to include an exemption for some sex offenders to be removed from the registry if they meet certain conditions, specifically related to age at the time of offense. Webber voted against the final version of the bill because it included this weaker language that he did not support, indicating that his original vote was in favor of a stronger version of the bill.

journalist_explanation: The NRCC ad says that Shea-Porter "votes with Nancy Pelosi’s Democrats 95 percent of the time," but Guinta "will take on both parties" and has "independent New Hampshire values." That’s a pretty stark comparison -- yet by the most apples-to-apples measurement of how both candidates have voted in Congress, Guinta scored a 96 percent partisan unity with Republicans during his term in Congress, which is hardly evidence of a big contrast. We rate the claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that Frank Guinta has also voted in virtual partisan lockstep, voting with his party at a rate of 96 percent in the current Congress (as per the Washington Post vote study) and 97-95 percent in previous years (per Congressional Quarterly), which is barely distinguishable from Rep. Carol Shea-Porter's voting record.

journalist_explanation: Obama said, "Since 2010, America has put more people back to work than Europe, Japan, and all advanced economies combined." From publicly available data, we know that since 2010, the United States has created more jobs than the 35 other advanced economies combined. However, it’s not as clear cut that this recovery involves putting "more people back to work," as Obama suggests. The labor force participation rate has consistently declined during this period, suggesting that more and more unemployed Americans are dropping out of the workforce, rather than taking new jobs. On balance, we rate Obama's claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided supports the claim that, in terms of net job creation, the United States has outperformed other advanced economies since 2010. However, when considering the percentage growth rate and population differences among these countries, the U.S. ranks lower than several nations on the IMF's list of advanced economies. Furthermore, the wording "put more people back to work" implies a specific definition of job creation, which may not align with the White House's use of net employment gain. Additionally, some experts question the accuracy of crediting President Obama for economic growth, highlighting that recessions can naturally lead to significant job recovery.

journalist_explanation: Kathleen Sullivan said the proportion of Rhode Islanders entering substance abuse treatment, primarily for marijuana, has reached its highest point in 20 years. Her documentation shows a peak in 2009, but then admissions decline through 2011. More recent data show the decline has continued. Further, our trend analysis shows no increase since 1999. And a federal statistician at the agency that compiled the data said admission rates have been "relatively stable" over the past 20 years. We rate her statement False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that while there was a peak in marijuana-related admissions in 2009 at 218 per 100,000 Rhode Islanders age 12 and older, this was not in 2011 or more recent years. Sullivan's statement referred to the overall trend in marijuana admissions, which according to the data has been increasing over the past two decades. However, when examining the trend line since 1999, there is no statistically significant increase. The officials from the U.S. Substance Abuse & Mental Health Services Administration also stated that the data does not support Sullivan's assertion that the number of Rhode Islanders entering substance abuse treatment primarily due to marijuana use has reached its highest point in 20 years, citing limitations with the data such as individuals being counted multiple times per year.

journalist_explanation: Trump claims that in early 2000, almost two years before the Sept. 11 attacks, "I wrote about Osama bin Laden: ‘We’ve got to take him out.’" Trump’s book did not contain those words or their clear likeness. Bin Laden’s name appears once in the book, when the author was criticizing the Clinton administration for having an unfocused national security policy. He complained that the U.S. kept shifting its military focus between Iraq, bin Laden’s organization and Kosovo without strong results. The book says that if bin Laden was "public enemy number one" in 1998, then the U.S. should have spent more than one day that year on a retaliatory bombing mission against his camps that bin Laden escaped. But Trump, never known for mincing words, did not call for future efforts to exterminate bin Laden or strike against al-Qaida. So we rate Trump’s hyperbolic statement Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from Donald Trump's book "The America We Deserve" shows that while bin Laden is mentioned in the book as part of a criticism of President Clinton's national security policy, there is no passage where Trump says "We've got to take him out." This contradicts Trump's claim about writing about Osama bin Laden and calling for his elimination.

journalist_explanation: Obama has discussed the need for the country to achieve energy independence through reduced consumption and more renewable energy sources. At times he connected those policies to lower gas prices for families. But he never promised a particular price point and certainly not $2.50 a gallon. We rate Curry’s statement False. PolitiFact Florida is partnering with 10 News for the 2012 election season. See the video version of this fact-check here.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that Barack Obama did not promise gasoline at $2.50 a gallon when he was running for office in 2008. In fact, the article quotes Obama as saying "I want to invest that money in clean, affordable, renewable energy sources... so that we're not talking about high fuel prices next summer or the next summer after that or the summer after that", which is far from pledging a particular price. Additionally, Obama's campaign promises were tracked by PolitiFact's Obameter and there is no evidence of him making such a promise.

journalist_explanation: Rubio, arguing to defund Obamacare, said "75 percent of small businesses now say they are going to be forced to either fire workers or cut their hours." That’s not remotely true. In the study of small businesses he cited, less than 10 percent said they might make that choice. His office cited a news article that misinterpreted ambiguous results from an interest-group survey. But basic statistics about America’s small businesses show the number was seriously unlikely, and a quick message to the U.S. Chamber exposed the error. Yet opinion pieces under Rubio’s name repeat the claim — one that’s so wrong, it’s ridiculous. We rate it Pants on Fire.
generated_explanation: The claim that 75 percent of small businesses will be forced to either fire workers or cut their hours under Obamacare is based on misinterpretation of a survey conducted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The actual data from the survey shows that only 17 percent of the executives said they would be affected by the employer mandate, and among those, between 5% and 9% planned to cut back hours or replace full-time workers.

journalist_explanation: The Americans for Tax Reform flyer said the Obama administration funneled about $2 billion in "green" stimulus money to foreign companies, with particular benefits for China.On the dollars, the claim understates the amount that went to foreign owned companies. It was certainly more than $2 billion, which would bolster the group’s claim.But the flyer offers a very selective picture of what the stimulus did for American workers..The distinction between domestic and foreign companies and the impact of that on jobs is unclear. And while the stimulus did help pay for high-skilled jobs overseas, it also leveraged thousands of jobs in the U.S. and produced earnings greater than the amount of money spent by the government. Money did leave the country, but not with the impact the flyer presents.Regarding China, the flyer exaggerates the benefits for that nation. China stood to gain from spending on solar power, and it is hard to see how it wouldn’t have collected millions of taxpayer dollars. But solar represented about a fifth of the stimulus subsidies. The wind projects accounted for 70 percent and in wind, China played a tiny role. The countries that gained the most overall were European.The statement has an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. We rate it Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided by the Investigative Reporting Workshop and the National Renewable Energy Laboratory confirms that a significant portion of the "green" stimulus money, around $2.4 billion, went to foreign companies with a substantial amount being used for overseas production, resulting in limited high-skill jobs in the United States.

journalist_explanation: Crist said, "Women in Florida make 83 cents for every dollar a man makes." The figure came from a think tank using 2011 Census annual median wage data, and was bumped up a penny to 84 cents for 2012 in its latest statement on the issue. While there are other ways to evaluate the difference between what each gender earns, with several reasons why that’s the case, the Census numbers are one widely accepted measure. We rate the claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: According to the provided evidence from the National Partnership for Women & Families (based on a 2011 American Community Survey report) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, women in Florida make around 83 cents or 84 percent of what men make, although there is some variation in estimates depending on the source and method used.

journalist_explanation: Carolyn Medeiros of the Alliance for Safe Communities said, "There's a tax credit of $2,400 to bond [former inmates] that an employer would get for hiring a convicted felon. There's a federal bonding program -- you can get $5,000 to $25,000 in federal money to hire a convicted felon. And there's federal grants for felons to set up their own small businesses."She was mostly correct about the tax credit (although it doesn't involve a bond). But she was wrong on the other two points.Because her statement contains some element of truth but gets some critical facts wrong, we rate it Mostly False.(If you have a claim you’d like PolitiFact Rhode Island to check, e-mail us at [emailprotected] And follow us on Twitter: @politifactri.
generated_explanation: According to Medeiros' own sources, there are no grants set up to help felons start their own small businesses. Additionally, while employers do receive a free bond through the Federal Bonding Program, they do not get $5,000 to $25,000 in federal money as Medeiros stated. The Work Opportunity Tax Credit is real and worth up to $2,400, but it's referred to as a tax credit, not a bonding program, and has certain restrictions.

journalist_explanation: Bush said in 2002, he "won more Hispanic votes than Anglo votes, 60 percent in the state." While Bush historically had enjoyed a strong Hispanic voter base, we found there actually aren’t the usual exit poll results from his 2002 re-election to support this conclusion. However, most media analyses from the election do suggest Bush carried about 60 percent of the Hispanic vote, as he did in 1998. Experts we consulted said that was most likely the case. The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information. We rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: While some independent analyses suggest that Jeb Bush won around 57-65% of the Hispanic vote in 2002, the evidence also shows that an exit poll was flawed and not kept for reference, making it difficult to determine the exact percentage. Additionally, there is no clear data from official sources such as Voter News Service to confirm or refute the claim.

journalist_explanation: Dewhurst said: "I have cut taxes 63 times, including a 2006 property tax reduction that ranks as the largest in state history." This statement paints an incomplete picture. About 63 (or 54) measures giving someone a tax break passed into law on Dewhurst’s watch, but it's not like Texans are less tapped by such taxes of late than before. Notably, too, most of the touted laws targeted particular beneficiaries. Also, Dewhurst didn't personally cut any taxes; those decisions involved the House, Senate and governor, though Dewhurst was a leader. The 2006 school property-tax-rate reduction was historic. But this statement fails to acknowledge that actions Dewhurst helped usher into place the same year led to hundreds of millions of dollars in lesser tax increases. All told, this claim contains an element of truth, but overlooks critical facts that would give a full, accurate impression. We rate it as Mostly False. MOSTLY FALSE – The statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: While Dewhurst did support tax-cut proposals passed into law on his watch, he had no vote on these measures, which belonged to senators and House members. The claim that he "has cut taxes 63 times" is an exaggeration, as he was more of a facilitator in the legislative process rather than a direct cutter of taxes.

journalist_explanation: Seaman says Nelson voted "yes on the pro-amnesty SJR 21, a bill urgingCongress to provide citizenship for those residing illegally in our country." To be clear, the "bill" was actually a resolution that holds no teeth. It calls fora pathway to citizenship for people not legally in the country. But it's too vague to blankly sayit falls under the "amnesty" umbrella, and just doesn’t mean much in the grand scheme of the immigration debate. We rate the claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, Erv Nelson voted for Senate Joint Resolution 21 (SJR 21), which urges Congress to provide citizenship for those residing illegally in our country and includes a clear path to citizenship. The resolution clearly spells out this point, making it an accurate claim that Nelson voted for a bill supporting a pathway to citizenship.

journalist_explanation: The website New Century Times said in a December headline that "Breaking: FBI just raided the White House, 6 people thrown out." Yes, six White House staffers were removed from their jobs due to problems associated with their in depth background checks, Politicoreported. But their removals occurred in February -- this isn’t "breaking" news in December. And it seems a stretch to describe the removals as an FBI "raid." We rate this claim False.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that the story about an FBI raid on the White House was exaggerated and dramatized by the New Century Times website. According to the evidence, the actual event was a routine removal of six staffers who failed background investigations, with no involvement of armed personnel or a sudden "raid" as described in the misleading headline.

journalist_explanation: :Guinta claims that "in the House of Representatives, we have 40 different jobs bills that have passed and almost all of them have been bipartisan."The House of Representatives has indeed passed more than 40 bills that Republicans consider jobs legislation. But whether they are truly "bipartisan" depends on your definition.Thirty-eight of them had support from at least one Democrat. But, according to political analysts, one vote does not a bipartisan bill make. Political analysts and academics alike commonly refer to Congressional Quarterly’s definition of a bipartisan bill as one that receives majority support from both parties. Only a fraction of the 42 bills referenced by Guinta meet that standard -- six to be exact. And even if you lower the threshold to 25 percent, it's only 10 bills.Guinta makes a sweeping claim that suggests broad support for nearly every bill. But in fact, the levels for bipartisanship are pretty skimpy. We rate this claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided is conflicting because U.S. Rep. Frank Guinta claims that almost all of the 40 different jobs bills passed in the House of Representatives were bipartisan, but according to Cantor's list and searches of THOMAS, at least 38 received some level of support from both parties, with only six meeting Congressional Quarterly Roll Call's 50 percent standard for bipartisanship. Political scientists and analysts provide alternative definitions of bipartisanship, which challenge Guinta's definition, and many question whether bills that receive only a handful of votes from the minority party can be considered truly bipartisan.

journalist_explanation: Gingrich warned that under Obama, the EPA plans to raise gasoline prices by 25 cents a gallon.He drew that information from an industry-funded study considering the cost impacts of the EPA’s proposed Tier 3 fuel standards and went right for the high end of the estimate. "Surely he knows that API has a vested interest in presenting a high projection," said Jenkins, of Republicans for Environmental Protection.Even more importantly, the study concluded its cost estimates based on fuel-standard changes that EPA is not considering. When looking only at lowering the sulfur content of gasoline, the cost would be far lower -- even less than a penny per gallon, according to a study commissioned by an environmental group. Gingrich’s statement exaggerates and misleads, and we rate it False.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that the EPA's proposal for Tier 3 regulations aims to reduce tailpipe pollution and does not specifically target a 25-cent-per-gallon increase in gasoline prices. The oil industry-sponsored study cited by Gingrich assumes changes in both sulfur content and RVP, but the EPA has since stated it is only exploring changes in sulfur levels.

journalist_explanation: Rubio said in the Senate debate "in about three weeks over a half million Floridians are going to lose their coverage again" through Obamacare. That’s a reference to more than 400,000 Floridians who are expected to lose their plans under the Obamacare exchange. However, Rubio omits that they will be offered another plan including by Florida Blue, which will remain in every county in Florida. Rubio also ignores the fact that due to the marketplace, 1.7 million Floridians have signed up for coverage -- larger than the more than 400,000 who will have to switch plans. The percentage of Floridians who are uninsured has been dropping under Obamacare in recent years. We rate this claim Half True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided by Bloomberg News and the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, approximately 420,000 enrollees in Florida are expected to lose their plans due to withdrawals in the individual exchange marketplace. Additionally, Karen Kees, a spokeswoman for the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, stated that this number is expected to be higher when including off-exchange enrollees who will also lose coverage. Rubio's statement that over half a million Floridians are going to lose their coverage again aligns with these numbers, suggesting his claim is true.

journalist_explanation: Rogers said, "In 2014, Mexico alone received over $24 billion in remittances sent from the U.S., while other South and Central American countries received over 15 percent of their GDPs in the form of remittances." Based on World Bank estimates, Mexico did receive more than $24 billion in remittances from the United States in 2015 (the year Rogers meant to use). Rogers would have been on safer ground in the second part of his statement had he described nations south of the border more generally. According to the latest data, a couple of countries in Central America — El Salvador and Honduras — received at least 15 percent of their GDP from remittances. Haiti, in the Caribbean, also received at least 15 percent. No country from South America reached that threshold. We rate Rogers' statement Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence confirms that Mexico received over $24 billion in remittances from the U.S. in 2014, as stated by Rep. Mike Rogers. However, it contradicts his claim that other South and Central American countries received more than 15 percent of their GDP in remittances, providing specific examples of countries like Haiti, Honduras, and El Salvador, which do not meet this threshold. Additionally, the text mentions a World Bank report showing Mexico received more than $25.6 billion in remittances from the U.S. in 2015, further confirming Rogers' statement about Mexico but not supporting his claim for other South and Central American countries.

journalist_explanation: Rubio said that for people who currently have health insurance, "They have a doctor they’ve been seeing for the last 15 or 20 years, they won’t be able to keep going to that doctor," due to Obamacare. Rubio ignores the fact that without Obamacare, patients can lose access to their doctor when their employer switches plans or they switch (or lose) jobs. Some patients who buy health insurance through the exchange could lose access to their current doctor, but it’s difficult to predict how many. We rate this claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that people who have a doctor they've been seeing for 15 or 20 years may still be able to keep going to that doctor under Obamacare, although there is a possibility of involuntary changes due to factors such as plan switching and exchange participation. However, experts like Gail Wilensky and Judith Stein emphasize that these scenarios were already present in the pre-Obamacare system, and it's difficult to predict how many people will be affected. Moreover, there are various factors at play, including payment rates and network participation, which make it challenging to determine a specific outcome.

journalist_explanation: In the debate, Romney cited the report’s headline figure pretty accurately. But he failed to note, first, that it was an estimate subject to significant uncertainty, and second, that the report itself included an alternative -- and arguably more accurate -- measurement that produced a significantly lower figure.That said, the lower figure, even when adjusted for uncertainty, still backs up Romney’s underlying point that illegal immigrants have gained a disproportionate share of new jobs in Texas. It’s just that the number probably isn’t as high as Romney said in the debate. So we rate the statement Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that Romney's statement is based on a study by the Center for Immigration Studies, which found that about 40 percent of job growth in Texas since 2007 went to newly arrived illegal immigrants. However, critics point out methodological shortcomings and assumptions made in the report, such as using gross numbers instead of net numbers and estimating the percentage of illegal immigrants. Additionally, experts agree that trying to draw conclusions from the data is problematic due to other factors at play. Therefore, it cannot be determined for certain whether the claim is true or false based on the evidence provided.

journalist_explanation: A Facebook post said, "ICE has not deported or detained one white illegal immigrant." The Facebook post does not include a source for its claim. ICE said it does not track the race of the people it removes from the country. Latin American countries were the top destinations where people were deported to in 2018. Hispanics or Latinos can be of any race, including white. News reports have noted that white immigrants have been detained and deported by ICE during Trump’s presidency. We rate the Facebook post False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that white immigrants have indeed been detained and deported by ICE. Specifically, it cites cases such as John Cunningham and Dylan O'Riordan, who were both from Ireland and had overstayed their visas or admission terms, leading to their detention and deportation. Additionally, the article mentions that Pew Research Center estimated 700,000 unauthorized people aged 18 and older in the US were white (not Hispanic), indicating the existence of a white population within this group.

journalist_explanation: Santorum said the federal government allows health insurance companies to keep only 15 percent of their revenues to run their businesses.His description of the medical loss ratio provision of the health reform law doesn't tell the whole story. The rule does require large group insurance plans to spend 85 percent of their premium income on real health care. For small group plans the rule is more generous. All health insurance companies are still free to spend other streams of revenue however they wish, and several types of expenses are specifically exempted from the 15 (or 20) percent limit.Santorum’s statement leaves out a good deal of important information. That pushes the needle to Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence confirms that the federal government has a regulation in place, known as the medical loss ratio, which requires most health insurance companies to spend at least 80 or 85 percent of their premium income on healthcare claims and quality improvement. This means that they are allowed to keep only 15 or 20 percent for administration, marketing, and profit.

journalist_explanation: Scott said that his proposal would allow "a potential of 168 hours, which I think is the most we’ve ever had" for early voting. He’s right that his proposal would give supervisors of elections the option to offer 168 hours of early voting, and that would be a record. We should note that supervisors would also have the option to only offer 48 hours of voting, which is less than previous law. But Scott was very careful with his wording, noting that 168 hours was the maximum and outlining the specific days and hours.
