A claim from his critics, Pink Slip Rick, said the law "only mandates 48 hours of early voting." We rated that Mostly True, because it didn't leave open the possibility of more hours. Scott's statement, on the other hand, specifically notes that the 168 hours are a maximum.Scott chose his words carefully and precisely. We rate his statement True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that voters had a maximum of 96 hours (14 days multiplied by 8 hours) and a minimum of 48 hours (8 days multiplied by 6 hours) under the previous laws. Scott's proposal would allow for up to 168 hours, but it is not stated in the article that this was not already possible under previous laws. However, it is mentioned that some supervisors welcomed the idea of tailoring early voting to their county's needs and considered it "nice to have the option" of going above 96 hours. This suggests that the claim might be an exaggeration or misrepresentation of what Scott's proposal actually does.

journalist_explanation: Teachers did get a salary increase in each of the past five years under Republican leadership. However, despite the "Held Harmless" statute, teachers who reach 25 years of experience or more today would not make as much as they would have in 2013-14. That’s the main wrinkle in Lee’s claim. North Carolina ranked second in fastest-rising teacher pay in 2016-17, though the ranking wasn’t consistent over the years. We rate this claim Mostly True. This story was produced by the North Carolina Fact-Checking Project, a partnership of McClatchy Carolinas, the Duke University Reporters’ Lab and PolitiFact. The NC Local News Lab Fund and the International Center for Journalists provide support for the project, which shares fact-checks with newsrooms statewide.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while average teacher salaries may have increased every year after 2013-14, teachers with 35 years of experience and those who reach that milestone were actually included in a category where their base salary was reduced or "held harmless" by the 2014-15 "Held Harmless" statute. Additionally, first-year teachers did not see an increase to their base salary after the 2015-16 academic year. However, according to the National Education Association, North Carolina was ranked second in having the fastest teacher pay raise in 2016-17 nationally. The information provided by Sen. Lee's legislative assistant suggests that he may have gotten his information from this ranking, which supports the claim that teacher pay increased under Republican leadership every year for the past 5 years. However, the detailed breakdown of salaries and the "Held Harmless" statute complicate the picture and suggest that teacher pay may not have actually increased for all teachers, leading to a conflicting assessment.

journalist_explanation: Santorum said if the United States raises the minimum wage to $10.10 an hour, "half a million people would lose their jobs." Santorum said "would"but really the 500,000-job figure wasthe CBO’s best guess. Analysts say job losses could be anywhere from just a few workers to as many as 1 million. Santorum's statement is accurate but needs clarification. We rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided is a direct quote from the February 2014 Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report, which states that "the economy would shed 500,000 jobs by the second half of 2016" if the federal minimum wage were gradually increased to $10.10 an hour for all workers.

journalist_explanation: Mack’s ad puts a lot of spin on the basic facts when it says, "George LeMieux was one of only two liberal Republicans who voted for Barack Obama’s liberal jobs bill that failed to help our economy." Certainly that "liberal" tag is what gives the ad its bite.Here, we’re simply checking whether LeMieux was one of two Republican senators who voted for a jobs bill supported by the president. That is the case. We rate that statement True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from the MSNBC's Morning Joe interview and LeMieux's statement to a reporter that he supported the Small Business Jobs and Credit Act of 2010, citing its benefits for small businesses in Florida, indicates that he indeed voted for Obama's jobs bill.

journalist_explanation: Clinton said, "President Obama took more money from Wall Street in the 2008 campaign than anybody ever had." Adjusting for inflation, Obama garnered about $3 million more than George W. Bush if you look at the broad "finance, insurance and real estate" sector. But using the "securities and investment" category, a tighter measure of Wall Street contributions, Obama clearly set a new record in 2008. Yet that record only lasted four years.Romney upped that ante by $5 million in 2012. Because the statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information, we rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided by the Center for Responsive Politics shows that President Obama received $17.3 million in 2008 from the "securities and investment" category, which is considered a good measure of Wall Street contributions. This amount exceeds the $10 million received by George W. Bush in 2004 ($11.4 million in 2008 dollars) and establishes Obama as having taken more money from Wall Street than anybody else in the 2008 campaign.

journalist_explanation: Axelrod said, "8.5 million Americans have gotten rebate checks because their insurance companies were spending too much money on executive bonuses and administrative costs and not enough on health care." He is correct on the number of rebates. However, like Obama before him, Axelrod’s claim isn’t clear on the fact that these checks are mostly going to employers who run plans for their workers, not individual Americans. Employers can then choose to pay their employees in a lump sum, reduce future premiums or act by "applying the rebate in a manner that benefits its employees," such as shoring up the health fund or offering better benefits. We rate the statement Mostly True.
generated_explanation: While 8.85 million policyholders were due rebates in 2013, about one-third (2.9 million people) physically received checks. The rest of the rebates went to employers who would then share or apply them proportionately with their employees, rather than being distributed directly as a check to policyholders.

journalist_explanation: Menendez said, "A white family is likely to have about six times as much wealth than a black or Hispanic family coming out of the recession." A study from the Urban Institute supports her statistic. Other research shows an even wider gap, further proving her point that race is a factor in U.S. wealth. Menendez's statement is accurate, and might even understate the issue. We rate her claim True.
generated_explanation: According to a report by the Urban Institute, which PunditFact found to be correct, for every $1 in wealth that an average black or Hispanic person has post-recession, an average white person has $6. Additionally, multiple experts, including Thomas Shapiro and Alicia Menendez, corroborated this ratio of 6-to-1 as accurate, although noting it may represent the lower end of a range of possible ratios (from 6-to-1 to 22-to-1).

journalist_explanation: Arene-Morley said that "There are more African American men in prison, jail, on probation or parole than were enslaved in 1850." Our research found that U.S. Bureau of Criminal Statistics put the number of African American men under state and federal criminal justice supervision in 2013 at about 1.68 million -- 807,076 above the number of African American men enslaved in 1850. The Sentencing Project, too, puts that number at 1.88 million with local jails factored in. Given that evidence, we rate Arene-Morley’s claim True. (If you have a claim you’d like PolitiFact Rhode Island to check, email us at [emailprotected] And follow us on Twitter: @politifactri.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided by the Department of Justice's Bureau of Justice Statistics, as well as Marc Mauer from The Sentencing Project, there were approximately 1.68 million African-American men under state and federal criminal justice supervision in 2013, which is more than the number of African-American men who were enslaved in 1850 (approximately 872,924).

journalist_explanation: Obama said 50 percent of CEOs are delaying hiring due to the shutdown, which accurately cites the results of a poll sponsored by the Business Roundtable. The survey’s limited sampling, though, means the responses aren’t necessarily representative of all U.S. businesses. But the idea that the shutdown affects how businesses think about hiring is more broadly applicable. Experts said it’s reasonable that CEOs would be hesitant to hire, given that uncertainty about government fiscal policy can affect consumer confidence.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that Business Roundtable conducted a survey among its 134 member CEOs (representing 63% of its total membership) and found that 50% of them indicated that the shutdown had a negative impact on their plans to hire additional employees over the next six months. While it's noted that the sample does not reflect a random selection of U.S. businesses, the survey results align with President Obama's claim, and an independent business group (National Federation of Independent Businesses) reports similar sentiment among its smaller business owners.

journalist_explanation: In the caption of a video posted to Facebook, Wooten said, "My opponent, Rick Gunn, blocked the expansion of Medicaid — costing half a million people health insurance, including at least 23,000 veterans." Wooten is mostly correct on the first two charges and close to correct on the third. Gunn co-sponsored a 2013 bill that rejected Medicaid expansion, so even if he was not solely responsible for blocking expansion, he played a role in it. Experts agree this is costing approximately 500,000 North Carolinians the chance at receiving health coverage. That would include many veterans, although the exact number is less clear than Wooten suggested. But given the available research, Wooten’s number seems reasonable. We rate this statement Mostly True. This story was produced by the North Carolina Fact-Checking Project, a partnership of McClatchy Carolinas, the Duke University Reporters’ Lab and PolitiFact. The NC Local News Lab Fund and the International Center for Journalists provides support for the project, which shares fact-checks with newsrooms statewide.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided supports the claim that Rick Gunn blocked the expansion of Medicaid and estimates suggest that withholding Medicaid expansion was costing half a million North Carolinians health insurance, including at least 23,000 veterans. Experts such as David Anderson and Lisa Dubay agreed with the estimate, and although the numbers may vary slightly, it does not seem to oversell the impact Medicaid expansion could have.

journalist_explanation: Shapiro said that a majority of Muslims are radicals. To make his numbers work, he had to cherry-pick certain results from public opinion surveys. Given the choice between two possible percentages, he chose the higher one. Shapiro also relied heavily on the idea that anyone who supported sharia law is a radical. Some of the best polling work shows that Muslim beliefs are much more nuanced. Some countries where high percentages of Muslims support Sharia law show low support for suicide attacks on civilians. Large fractions of Muslims that endorse sharia law do not want it imposed on others. The meaning of Sharia law varies from sect to sect and nation to nation. Shapiro’s definition of radical is so thin as to be practically meaningless and so too are the numbers he brings to bear. We rate the claim False.
generated_explanation: The article presents evidence showing that alternative measures of radicalism yield significantly lower numbers than Shapiro's claim. The table provided demonstrates how different criteria for measuring radicalism, such as support for suicide bombings or Sharia law, result in estimates ranging from 19% to 72% of Muslims worldwide being considered "radical". This suggests that Shapiro's conclusion, which represents a majority of Muslims as radicals, is an outlier and likely inflated due to the use of a broad and somewhat ambiguous definition of radicalism.

journalist_explanation: The Texas Democratic Party’s spokeswoman correctly cited two figures from the 2011 NALEO directory suggesting that Latino elected Democrats in Texas greatly outnumber their Republican counterparts.Still, this claim is missing substantive context -- that NALEO did not determine the party memberships of most Latino Texas officeholders. If this were done, the Democratic-Republican ratio might change.We rate the claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided by the National Association of Latino Elected and Appointed Officials (NALEO) confirms that as of January 2011, there were 668 Democratic Hispanic elected officials to 60 Republican Hispanic elected officials in Texas.

journalist_explanation: Rove said Clinton spent 30 days in the hospital and then emerged wearing glasses that only people with traumatic brain injury use. Rove since said he was wrong about the length of her hospital stay. The actual number is four days. By describing a long hospital stay and tying it to signs of traumatic brain injury, Rove associated Clinton with a more profound medical episode. Experts reject that association. Concussions are the mildest form of traumatic brain injury. The glasses Clinton wore are an optional treatment for temporary problems of double vision that are relatively common among people who suffer concussions along with other conditions. She has not worn the glasses for some time, and the neurologists we contacted said most people recover fully. While Rove never claimed Clinton suffered brain damage, he was wrong about the hospital stay and combined that with the glasses to exaggerate the nature of Clinton’s injury. His claim is inaccurate. We rate it False.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, Hillary Clinton spent only about 4 days in the hospital in 2012 due to a stomach virus and blood clot, not 30 days as claimed by Rove. Additionally, experts and doctors confirmed that the glasses she wore were prismatic glasses designed to help with blurred or double vision caused by concussion, which is a common consequence of concussions, but not exclusive to traumatic brain injury.

journalist_explanation: Rubio said, "We have an Army that just cut 40,000 spots." Rubio was referring to an announcement by the Army in July that it will cut 40,000 spots by fiscal year 2018. Those cuts had been talked about for several months, but the specifics were released in July. The cuts will start this fall but are expected to continue under the next president. Since the end date is under a new president and Congress, it’s difficult to guess if they will all happen, but that’s the plan for now. We rate this claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence from Army officials confirms that they plan to cut the size of the regular Army from 490,000 to 450,000 by fiscal year 2018, which is a reduction of 40,000 spots.

journalist_explanation: Paul said Obama "spent nearly a trillion dollars on make-work government jobs." It’s plausible that through the stimulus, Obama spent nearly $1 trillion of taxpayer dollars in hopes it would create jobs. But Paul is wrong to suggest that all $1 trillion was spent on "make-work government jobs." Two-thirds of the stimulus was spent on tax cuts and entitlements, and of the remaining one-third, much was paid to private contractors. Only a modest fraction of the $1 trillion was spent on government jobs, much less on jobs spent doing nothing. We rate his claim False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that only a small fraction of the stimulus money went towards government employees and "make-work" jobs, with most funds allocated to tax benefits, entitlements, and private sector contracts. Additionally, government employment has actually declined by 734,000 jobs since Obama took office, which contradicts Paul's claim that President Obama "spent nearly a trillion dollars on make-work government jobs."

journalist_explanation: A post on Facebook claims that "AARP endorsed Biden" and "says if you are past 75 you should just die and go away." AARP didn’t endorse Biden, or anyone. And the organization, which represents millions of Americans age 50 and older, has aggressively lobbied against any health care policies that would discriminate against aging populations. We rate these claims about AARP Pants on Fire!
generated_explanation: The claim that AARP endorsed Biden and said people over 75 should "just die and go away" is contradicted by statements from an AARP spokesperson, press releases, and news coverage. These sources confirm that AARP opposes rationing care based on age or disability and does not endorse political candidates.

journalist_explanation: A viral image suggests that Donald Trump was only ever accused of racism after he decided to run for public office against Democrats. The record is clear, however, that Trump has deflected allegations that he is a racist since the 1970s and many times since. We rate this Facebook post False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that there have been numerous accusations of racism against Donald Trump throughout his public life, long before he decided to run against the Democrats. Articles from reputable sources such as the New York Times and Vox document specific incidents and quotes from Trump that demonstrate a history of racist behavior. These findings contradict the claim that Trump was never once accused of being racist until he ran against the Democrats.

journalist_explanation: Bush said that "as governor of Florida, I used a combination of strategies to help reduce heroin use among youth in Florida by approximately 50 percent." The only statistics that directly address his statement offer numeric support.However, the report in question cautions against drawing broad conclusions for such low-frequency events as youth heroin addiction, and experts thought it curious that the drop essentially happened in the first year, with little change after that. Experts praise Bush for his drug policies, but it’s important to note that broader demographic and social factors -- reflected in falling youth heroin use nationally during that period -- likely made a difference as well. We rate the claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided by the 2006 Florida Youth Substance Abuse Survey conducted by the Florida Department of Children and Families shows that there was indeed a 50% decrease in heroin use among youth in Florida between 2000 and 2006, both for lifetime use and for use in the past 30 days.

journalist_explanation: Cruz said, "One of the most troubling aspects of the Rubio-Schumer Gang of Eight bill was that it gave President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees, including Syrian refugees, without mandating any background checks whatsoever." The failed 2013 bill did not change the number of refugees, the overall framework of the screening process or give the president authority to admit any group at will. It would have allowed the president to designate certain groups outside the United States as particularly at risk, and other officials to label certain refugees in the United States as having nowhere to go. It further would have repealed the deadline for refugees already here to apply for asylum. Experts said none of the provisions Cruz has previously cited work the way he is warning they would. We rate his statement False.
generated_explanation: While the Rubio-Schumer Gang of Eight bill did give the president power to define who is considered "stateless" and grant refugee status, it did not give the president blanket authority to admit refugees without background checks. The evidence shows that all refugees would still be subject to background checks, interviews, and confirmation from several federal agencies.

journalist_explanation: Bush said that the three Republican senators running for president "have a combined two bills that became law that they've sponsored." Bush has his numbers right: Of all the bills Cruz, Rubio and Paul have sponsored combined, only two bills have been signed into law. But experts told us that this isn’t a great measurement of a legislator’s effectiveness, and there are other ways to show impact in Congress. All three senators have their fingerprints on numerous laws as cosponsors or amendment authors. We rate Bush’s claim Mostly True. Editor's note: This post has been updated to include a response from the Cruz campaign that we received after publishing the article and to clarify the senators identified by Bush in his claim.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided states that "We found that Bush’s statement is accurate in that the three senators have sponsored just two bills that eventually became law." This confirms that the claim is true.

journalist_explanation: At the Jacksonville debate, Gingrich was more accurate than he's been in the past and his chronology of the law and the four budgets is correct. But he oversimplifies the causes of the balanced budget. His words are accurate but need additional information, which makes this a Mostly True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided, during Gingrich's time as speaker from 1995-1999, there were deficits in fiscal years 1996 and 1997, but then two consecutive surpluses in fiscal years 1998 and 1999. However, the country ultimately did have four consecutive balanced budgets (fiscal years 1998 to 2001), which meets the condition stated in the claim.

journalist_explanation: In a radio interview, Christie claimed that in Obama’s first two years, the president had "huge majorities in the House and Senate, and did nothing with them to create jobs in America."But Obama and the Democratic-controlled Congress did do something, governor. It’s called the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, a stimulus bill that various economists credit with creating or saving jobs.That’s why it is ridiculous for Christie to claim Obama did "nothing." Pants on Fire! To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 allocated billions of dollars for federal spending and tax benefits, which led to the creation or saving of a significant number of jobs. Multiple economic research studies are cited as supporting this conclusion, including projections from organizations such as the Congressional Budget Office, Moody's Analytics, and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

journalist_explanation: Ratliff wrote that Massachusetts has three mandated student tests and Finland one.Both claims reflect the exams that students in Massachusetts and Finland have to take to qualify for high school graduation.But students on the academic track in Finland must take at least four separate tests. Also, given that Ratliff’s article does not say he’s speaking only to tests administered in high school, it’s worth noting that Massachusetts, like Texas, requires students starting in third grade to take state tests.This claim grades out as Half True. CLARIFICATION, 10:00 a.m., Dec. 19, 2012: We amended this article to point out that Finnish students who focus on vocational courses at the secondary level do not have to take a government-mandated exam to graduate. This wrinkle, brought to our attention by a reader, did not change our Truth-O-Meter rating.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that Massachusetts has state-mandated tests for high school students in English language arts, math, and a science-related subject, but also allows students who do not meet the "proficient" score to graduate with an educational proficiency plan. Additionally, students in grades 3-8 must take standardized state exams. This suggests that Massachusetts has more than one state-mandated test. However, the evidence also shows that Finland has a single exam at the end of high school, known as the Finnish Matriculation Exam, but this exam consists of "at least four tests" and students may choose to take additional optional tests, which can total up to 10 or more exams over a period of time. Therefore, it cannot be determined for certain whether Finland has only one state-mandated test.

journalist_explanation: Hassan said that there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold for confirming Supreme Court nominees." Most Supreme Court nominees have indeed reached 60 votes. But not all have, and the official standard remains 50 percent plus one, not 60. And while a 60-vote supermajority for cloture is often required these days for much of the Senate’s business, filing for cloture is actually the exception, not the rule, where recent Supreme Court nominations are concerned. Cloture votes have been required in only four of the 23 confirmations since the Eisenhower Administration. This calls into question Hassan’s use of the term "traditional." We rate the statement Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that while a cloture vote requires 60 votes to end debate and force a vote on a Supreme Court nominee, it is not the "traditional" threshold for confirming nominees. In fact, most Supreme Court nominations have been confirmed without a cloture vote, including those of Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, who received 68 and 63 votes respectively, but were never filibustered.

journalist_explanation: Anne Nolan said Rhode Islanders who have been homeless for at least a year cost Medicaid an average of $60,000 per person per year. But the $60,000 cost she cites applied only to the 67 homeless people with the highest medical bills, a major caveat she didn't mention in her commentary. The annual dollar amount for all Medicaid recipients in the study who were homeless for at least a year was $23,650 -- a substantial cost to taxpayers, but far less than what Nolan indicated. Because Nolan's statement makes it sound like it applies to all long-term homeless people on Medicaid when, in fact, it only focuses on the most-expensive subset, we rate it False. (If you have a claim you’d like PolitiFact Rhode Island to check, email us at [emailprotected] And follow us on Twitter: @politifactri.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that the $60,000 per person figure only applied to the 67 individuals who had the highest Medicaid bills among those who were homeless for one year or more, not the average cost for all long-term homeless people on Medicaid. When Eric Hirsch recalculated the data for the larger group of 442 long-term homeless people, he found that their average Medicaid charges per person per year was $23,650, which is still lower than the claimed $60,000.

journalist_explanation: On Morning Joe, Coburn said, "In 2010, everybody said you can't dare let guns go into the national parks, and of course the rapes, murders, robberies and assaults are down about 85 percent since we did that." Coburn’s office acknowledges that he misspoke; they actually calculated a decline of 12 percent, which is dramatically lower than 85 percent. But we find even the revised statistic to be questionable. It hinges on using 2008 data, when 2009 data would be more appropriate -- and a comparison using data from 2009 actually shows an increase in violent crime in national parks since the gun ban was lifted. Meanwhile, it’s far from clear that guns had an influence on the relatively small number of crimes that take place in national parks. We rate Coburn’s statement False.
generated_explanation: Coburn's office acknowledged that he overstated the decline in violent incidents by claiming an 85% drop, when in fact the data shows a 12% decrease. Additionally, upon examining the original data provided, it was found that murders actually went up between 2008 and 2011, and using 2008 as the "before" year amounts to cherry picking.

journalist_explanation: Clinton said that voters in Texas had to wait in long lines because "the Republican side gets 25 machines, the Democratic side gets five machines." Clinton is right that people in Texas waited for hours to vote, but she’s off on the polling machine disparity. In the county that experienced the longest lines on Super Tuesday, a main problem was the opposite of what Clinton described: a local decision to provide an equal number of machines for Republicans and Democrats at each voting location. We rate this claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while there were indeed long lines in Texas on Super Tuesday, the claim that "the Republican side gets 25 machines, the Democratic side gets 5 machines" is not supported. In fact, the article states that Harris County allocated an equal number of voting machines for each party at every polling place, which led to longer lines for Democratic voters due to their higher turnout. Additionally, Tarrant County's plan called for a set number of voting machines based on past voter turnout data, but this was not 25:5 ratio as claimed by Clinton.

journalist_explanation: Rosenberg made the claim that a Liberian woman is "more likely to be married by 18 than to know how to read." This claim relies on data from an old 2007 survey. Using a more recent survey and the closest age group for which data are available, the comparison doesn’t hold. Young Liberian women are more likely to know how to read than be married. We rate this claim Mostly False. This fact-check originally was published by Africa Check. Read their version of this story here.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided suggests that while a significant percentage of women in Liberia are married by age 18 (ranging from 35.9% based on 2013 survey data to potentially higher rates as implied by older statistics), the evidence for literacy rates is also inconclusive and varies depending on the definition used.

journalist_explanation: At a campaign event in New Hampshire last week, Christie claimed New Jersey lost private-sector jobs between 2000 and 2009 because Democrats increased taxes, fees, regulations and state spending.The governor’s right about the drop in private-sector jobs: New Jersey lost 155,000 jobs between December 1999 and December 2009. But the reasons behind those job losses are complex and Christie failed to acknowledge the impact of the recession, which coincided with the bulk of the job losses. We rate the statement Half True. To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence provides contradictory information regarding the claim. On one hand, it is stated that New Jersey did lose private-sector jobs between 2000 and 2009. However, the experts cited in the evidence argue that this loss cannot be attributed solely to tax increases, fee hikes, regulations, or state spending. They suggest that the recession played a significant role in the job losses, and other factors such as competitiveness also contributed to weak private-sector job growth. This conflicting information prevents a clear determination of whether the claim is true or false.

journalist_explanation: Adler said: "57% of the jobs created from 2009 to 2013 do not pay families a living wage." To be precise, that’s the estimated share of net jobs added in the multi-county Austin area (not Austin alone) pegged as having median wages less than the living wage for an adult with one child. Families vary in size, though, as do related living wages. We rate this statement, which lacks clarification, Mostly True. MOSTLY TRUE – The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that according to the data compiled by EMSI and cited by the Austin American-Statesman, approximately 57% of the newly created jobs from 2009 to 2013 paid less than the living wage for a single parent with one child ($19.56 per hour). Additionally, independent analysis by Cynthia Osborne and Daniel Dillon using more detailed data confirmed that around 57% of the jobs added in the Austin area did not pay the living wage for an adult with one child.

journalist_explanation: Sanders said that if American multinational corporations had to pay taxes on the profits they made overseas, they would owe $620 billion. This is at the high end of the estimates we collected. Sanders also described the overseas holdings as cash. According to one expert we reached, a lot of that money might be invested in factories and other hard infrastructure and might not be available for tax collections. Still, the mid-range estimate from credible sources is in the $500 billion to $550 billion range. All the numbers cited were relatively high. We rate Sanders’ estimate Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided includes various expert opinions and estimates of the potential tax revenues, ranging from $300 billion to over $620 billion. While some experts, such as Richard Harvey, suggest that Sanders' estimate may be conservative, others, like Edmund Outslay, question the assumptions made in the study behind the estimate and provide lower estimates. This disagreement among experts indicates that it cannot be determined for certain whether the claim is true or false based on the evidence provided.

journalist_explanation: Clinton said, "Since we last debated in Las Vegas, nearly 3,000 people have been killed by guns." We found a few problems with her statement. First, we don’t actually know how many people have died in the last month. Clinton’s statement is based on 2013 data from the CDC, which tallied nearly 3,000 gun deaths per month that year. There’s not more recent data available. Experts say the number of gun deaths this year is likely to be similar to or higher than 2013, so Clinton’s claim is probably not too far off. But we can’t know for sure. Also, it’s likely that at roughly half of these deaths are due to suicide. It could be even higher. Clinton’s phrasing obscures that point. Clinton used very specific language even though she’s actually extrapolating from old data. Overall, we rate her claim Half True. Editor's note: The Gun Violence Archive got back to us after publication, and we've updated the piece to include their comments.
generated_explanation: The claim that nearly 3,000 people have been killed by guns since the last debate in Las Vegas cannot be supported by the evidence provided. Although the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) data shows a monthly average of approximately 2,800 gun deaths in 2013, it is mentioned that Clinton was referring to 2015, not 2013. Moreover, the Gun Violence Archive's numbers, which are less comprehensive and do not include suicides, also do not support the claim. The experts consulted for this article agree that while the number of gun deaths in 2015 might be higher than in 2013 due to increased homicides and suicides, it is impossible to confirm if nearly 3,000 people have been killed by guns since the Las Vegas debate.

journalist_explanation: In this statement, Coons suggested that that ACA provided pre-existing condition protections to the more than 150 million Americans who get their health coverage through their place of employment. But that is not completely correct.Those were already in place through HIPAA, though expanded by the ACA. We rate Coons’ statement as Half True.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence, protections against preexisting condition discrimination for most people with job-based insurance predated the ACA by more than a decade, thanks to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA). HIPAA protected those continuously covered under employer plans from being denied coverage or charged waiting periods in new jobs. The ACA further addressed gaps left by HIPAA, including requiring large employers to provide a minimum package of benefits and insurers to sell policies to individuals with preexisting conditions without charging them more.

journalist_explanation: Christie said: "property taxes went up 70 percent in the 10 years before I became governor."In the decade before Christie took office, the average property tax bill climbed more than 70 percent, from roughly $4,240 to about $7,280.But when property tax rebates are taken into account, the increase is less, jumping roughly 50 percent in a decade.Either way, Christie is on point that property taxes increased significantly from 1999 to 2009.We rate this statement Mostly True.To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that the average property tax bill in New Jersey increased from $4,240 in 1999 to $7,280 by 2009, a more than 71 percent increase. However, when property tax rebates are factored in, the increase is roughly 51 percent.

journalist_explanation: The cyber-squatter site claims that after laying off "30,000 people," Carly Fiorina said that in retrospect, "I would have done them all faster." While the number is accurate -- acknowledged in a 2006 interview by Fiorina -- the comment that "I would have done them all faster" is pulled out of context. In fact, Fiorina was more specifically referring to her decisions to force out a small number of top-level executives, not tens of thousands of rank-and-file employees. The claim is partially accurate, but takes some things out of context, so we rate it Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that Carly Fiorina did indeed say she would have done some layoffs "faster", but it's not clear if this specifically refers to the 30,000 people laid off. In one quote, Fiorina mentions firing certain high-ranking executives quickly and says "I would have done them all faster" - implying that she is referring to a smaller group of individuals rather than the entire 30,000 people laid off.

journalist_explanation: It’s hard to say exactlyhow many failing schools are in North Carolina, but we do know there are not 500 like AFP state director Donald Bryson said. He was referring to low-performing schools, but the majority of low-performing schools are D schools – which most people don’t consider failing. We counted failing schools in a number of ways, with the results ranging from 80 to 415 depending on the grading scale used to define what an F is. Any way you slice itthere are clearly dozens, and maybehundreds, of failing schools statewide. Bryson’s statement was overly broad, but it’s not totally wrong. We rate this claim Half True.
generated_explanation: Although the state's definition of "low-performing" includes F schools as well as D schools, an expert on education policy notes that the grading system is flawed and punishes schools for having students who came to them below grade level. Furthermore, nearly half of the schools Bryson considers failing are actually improving, and a range of estimates (80-415) indicates that the number of truly failing schools is significantly lower than 500.

journalist_explanation: Cruz said, 70 percent of Republicans nationwide "don't think Donald Trump is the right guy" to take on Hillary Clinton in November. Cruz is referring to the polling average of 34 percent of GOP voters who say Trump is their top choice. Inverted, 66 percent of Republicans prefer someone else. That doesn’t mean, however, that the 66 percent refuse to support Trump overall. The highest estimate we found for Republicans flat-out protesting Trump is 42 percent. Cruz’s statement is largely accurate but leaves out some context. We rate it Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while it is true that a significant portion of Republicans do not prefer Donald Trump as their nominee, the actual percentage is unclear. Cruz's statement citing 70% of Republicans who don't think Trump is the right guy cannot be confirmed based on the polling data presented, which suggests a more nuanced and varied preference among Republican voters.

journalist_explanation: Trump said that 72 percent of the refugees admitted into United States between Feb. 3 and Feb. 11 were from seven countries his executive order targets. According to the Refugee Processing Center, of the 1,462 refugees entering the United States between that time frame, roughly 72 percent were from Syria, Iran, Iraq, Somalia, Syria and Sudan. No refugees were from Libya and Yemen. We rate Trump’s claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from the Refugee Processing Center's data shows that, during the period from February 3 to 11, approximately 72% (1,049 out of 1,462) of refugees admitted into the U.S. were indeed from the seven countries listed: SYRIA, IRAQ, SOMALIA, IRAN, SUDAN, LIBYA & YEMEN, which aligns with President Trump's statement.

journalist_explanation: Cruz said of Trump, "The one person he has suggested that would make a good justice is his sister, who is a court of appeals judge appointed by Bill Clinton. She is a hardcore pro-abortion liberal judge." Cruz’s claim is misleading. Yes, Trump said his sister would make a good Supreme Court justice. But he said he wouldn’t appoint her, and he has named two other potential nominees. And yes, Clinton elevated Trump’s sister to the appeals court. But Cruz leaves out that Reagan appointed her to the federal bench in the first place. Trump’s sister did join in ruling a New Jersey ban on partial-birth abortions unconstitutional. It’s worth noting that Justice Alito — hardly a "hardcore pro-abortion liberal judge" — joined in that opinion. Cruz twisted and left out facts to make a faulty claim about Trump’s views on the Supreme Court. We rate Cruz’s claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that while Donald Trump did suggest his sister Maryanne Trump Barry as a potential nominee, and described her as "phenomenal", he has also stated on multiple occasions that she is not the right person for the job due to their differing views. Furthermore, at a debate in South Carolina two days before Cruz's claim, Trump named Diane Sykes and Bill Pryor as alternative conservative nominees.

journalist_explanation: U.S. House candidate and State Rep. Jack Flanagan said that "almost 5 percent if not more" of the population of Coos and Sullivan counties were enrolled in the state’s expanded Medicaid program. In the second congressional district, one county has more than 5 percent enrollment in the state’s expanded Medicaid program and another is pretty close. Coos county indeed breaks the 5 percent mark. Sullivan, at 4.28 percent, which have the first and second-highest participation rates in the state, respectively. We rate Flanagan’s statement True.
generated_explanation: While it is true that Coos County has a participation rate above 5 percent in the expanded Medicaid program, Sullivan County's enrollment rate of 4.28 percent does not meet the claim's threshold of "almost 5 percent if not more".

journalist_explanation: Trump said, "Out of 67 counties (in Florida), I won 66, which is unprecedented. It's never happened before." Trump won 66 counties, but it’s far from unprecedented for Florida primary winners to win by a huge margin. Going back even just a few decades, there are several instances of candidates winning all 67 counties. We rate Trump’s statement Pants On Fire!
generated_explanation: Although Trump did win 66 out of 67 counties in the Republican primary, the evidence shows that winning all or nearly all counties is not unprecedented, as several instances in previous years (2004, 2000, 1996) demonstrate that other candidates and even Donald Trump himself in another contest beat his record.

journalist_explanation: Romney told donors he could win over wavering voters by reminding them that Obama said "he'd keep unemployment below 8 percent."Obama didn’t say that. Rather, his Council of Economic Advisers predicted that the stimulus would hold it to that level. Their report included heavy disclaimers that the projections had "significant margins of error" and a high degree of uncertainty due to a recession that is "unusual both in its fundamental causes and its severity."The sub-8 percent prediction did not hold true, but it’s still incorrect to characterize it as a promise or guarantee.We rate Romney’s statement Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that the report from Christina Romer and Jared Bernstein projected that the stimulus plan would result in unemployment rates peaking below 8% in 2009, but did not promise this outcome. However, the report also included disclaimers stating that their estimates are subject to significant margins of error and uncertainty. Additionally, the actual unemployment rate exceeded 8% and peaked at just over 10%.

journalist_explanation: In a panel discussion on HBO’s "Real Time with Bill Maher," Booker claimed that "right now, we have more military spending than the next 10, 11, 12 countries combined."The mayor’s statement is accurate, according to data from two leading authorities on worldwide military spending. One set of figures shows that, in 2011, military spending by the United States exceeded the combined total of the next 12 highest nations by roughly $40 billion.We rate the statement True. To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute and The International Institute for Strategic Studies shows that in 2011, the United States spent more on defense than the combined total of other high-spending nations. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the U.S. spent $711 billion, while the next top 12 spending nations accounted for a combined total of $670.9 billion. Similarly, The International Institute for Strategic Studies reports that the United States' defense budget in 2011 was $739.3 billion, making it the largest in the world, and the combined total of the next top 9 nations was $486.7 billion.

journalist_explanation: Napolitano said that "Woodrow Wilson borrowed $30 billion to fund World War I in 1917. That money has not been paid back. And we are still paying interest on it." The original Liberty Bonds and Victory Notes stopped paying interest decades ago. But Napolitano argues that, because the United States has never subsequently zeroed out its debt, the original World War I debt has been rolled over countless times, leaving subsequent bondholders to pay off a small, ancestral fraction of that old debt. That’s one way of looking at it, but not a view that carries much weight with experts, who call the rollover method straightforward and uncontroversial. We rate the claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that while Woodrow Wilson did borrow approximately $30 billion to fund World War I in 1917, this debt has not continued to accrue interest since its initial maturity. The Treasury Department "rolled over" the debt by selling new bonds to pay off the old ones as they matured, meaning that no specific current bond can be assigned to the historical incident of funding World War I. This is confirmed by experts such as Linda M. Hooks and Neil Buchanan, who agree that rolled-over debt does not mean ongoing interest payments on initial debt.

journalist_explanation: In the GOP radio address, Hutton said a "study showed as many as one in four people have had a package stolen from their residence." A trio of surveys of online shoppers supports that number, though statistics from law enforcement are hard to come by. We rate the claim True. How to avoid porch piracy Milwaukee Police Officer Jennifer Feather in a "Cyber Monday" message posted Dec. 2, 201,9 on the Nextdoor social network for neighborhoods, said porch piracy is preventable. "The Milwaukee Police Department wants to remind residents to be vigilant this holiday season as packages begin to arrive on our doorsteps." Feather also offered tips to neighbors to help thwart package thefts: 1. Keep each other updated about recent package theft activity 2. Share surveillance footage of a package theft in action 3. Ask a neighbor to pick up a package if your plans have you away from home 4. Offer to pick up a neighbor’s packages 5.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided from the "2019 Porch Package Theft Report" by Shorr Packaging Corp. states that nearly 1 in 4 online shoppers surveyed (24%) had personally experienced package theft, which supports Hutton's claim. Additionally, two other sources, Security.org and Canary, also report similar rates of package theft, with close to 40% and nearly 1 in 5 Americans being victims or knowing someone who was a victim, respectively.

journalist_explanation: Andrews said, "Missouri is actually the only state that has been forced to borrow money from the federal government to pay for unemployment benefits during each of the last five economic downturns." According to the data from the U.S. Department of Labor, not only did Missouri take out loans from the federal government to pay for unemployment benefits during economic downturns, but also it is the only state to do so. We rate this claim as True.
generated_explanation: According to the data from the U.S. Department of Labor, Missouri has borrowed money from the federal government in each of the last five economic downturns to make up for deficits in its unemployment trust fund. A review of data on borrowing by other 49 states confirms that Missouri is indeed the only state to receive a loan from the federal government during these time periods.

journalist_explanation: As CFO, Sink did watch the debt increase over her term, but by $3.4 billion, not $5.2 billion. Plus, the Legislature, not the Cabinet, has most of the say in bond appropriations. Not to mention there was a nationwide recession that took its toll on the Florida economy, which is out of the hands of state officials. Given all these hefty clarifications, we rate the Florida Republican Party of Florida’s claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided, when considering only Alex Sink's term as CFO (2007-2011), the increase in debt was $3.4 billion, not $5.2 billion as claimed by the Republican Party of Florida and referenced in the ad.

journalist_explanation: The mayor said that under his plan, half of the city’s residences would see a drop in water bills. His carefully worded statement is accurate. The unspoken part is that 50 percent will see their bills increase. The mayor also omits that his proposal would lead to a modest rate hike for the average water user. The mayor is correct, but his statement benefits from additional information. We rate the claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that under Mayor Dwight Jones' plan, the base rate charged to all customers for water and wastewater service would decrease by half, while the second monthly payment based on the volume of water used would rise. According to a chart sent by the mayor's spokeswoman, about 25,904 customers (about half of the city's residential customers) use 400 cubic feet or less each month, which means they would see lower bills due to the increase in their base rate being less than the savings from the halving of the base rate. Additionally, a report by Raftelis Financial Consultants shows that the average residential household uses 600 cubic feet of water and wastewater per month, which is above the threshold for the increased volume fee.

journalist_explanation: Tedisco said the measure raising the minimum wage for tipped workers in Maine was reversed in less than a year. Tedisco is right. Voters in Maine raised the minimum wage for tipped workers through a ballot initiative. State lawmakers reversed that decision less than a year later after pressure from restaurant workers who were against the wage increase. We rate his claim True.
generated_explanation: The claim states that Maine "reversed [the decision to raise the minimum wage for tipped workers] due to restaurant employees organizing en masse against the measure." However, according to the evidence, it was actually the Maine legislature that passed a new law in June 2017 making the minimum wage for tipped workers half of the regular minimum wage, after hundreds of restaurant owners and workers showed up at the state capitol to voice their opposition. This shows that while there was public opposition, the decision to reverse the original measure was made by lawmakers rather than solely due to employee organization.

journalist_explanation: Patrick said the 2014-15 state budget written by lawmakers and signed into law by Perry "cut border security and funding to fight criminal gangs." Yet his cited figures drew from budget summaries that did not show all border spending. Budgeted border security funding in 2014-15 exceeds the total in the 2012-13 budget by about one third, while budgeted 2014-15 spending on battling gangs has yet to be fully calculated. It’s a PolitiFact principle not to hold people responsible for information that wasn’t available when they made their claims. In this instance, though, our sense is Patrick could at least have pinned down total border security funding before he spoke. The fact that anti-gang spending has still not been totaled leaves Patrick’s claim with a possible element of truth. We rate the full statement as Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that budgeted border spending actually rose about $118 million from 2012-13 to 2014-15, contradicting Sen. Dan Patrick's claim that the state budget "cut border security and funding to fight criminal gangs."

journalist_explanation: Sundheim said California’s violent crime rate increased 34 percent over the past year, citing a recent report. Sundheim misread the report in question, its authors said. We rate his claim False. FALSE–The statement is not accurate. Click here formoreon the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) report cited by Sundheim does not support a 34% increase in violent crime in California. According to the PPIC, the preliminary data for January to June 2015 showed a double-digit percentage increase in violent crimes in 34 out of 66 cities, but there is no mention of a statewide 34% increase. Additionally, the PPIC's co-author and author stated that they did not see any data showing a 34% increase in crime in California for 2015.

journalist_explanation: Foster said that 60 percent of car thefts occur because the owner left keys inside the vehicle. In St. Petersburg this year, it’s actually 83.4 percent. An expert said that might be tops in the country. The specific number aside, Foster’s point that many auto thefts can easily be avoided is 100 percent on the mark. We rate this claim True.
generated_explanation: According to the Police Chief Chuck Harmon, out of 551 cars stolen so far this year, 460 had keys either in the ignition or elsewhere in the vehicle. That's 83.4 percent, not 60 percent as claimed by Mayor Foster and stated in the claim.

journalist_explanation: Kander said "Blunt voted to raise his own pay 12 times" while in Congress. This is a misleading attack. Blunt did not literally vote to increase his pay 12 times. He voted in support of measures that could have blocked or limited automatic cost-of-living increases from taking effect. Even all of those cases aren’t clear-cut, as sometimes Blunt sided with efforts to stop the automatic pay increase. Kander’s statement contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression. We rate it Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that Roy Blunt did not directly vote for 12 pay increases, but rather voted against measures to stop or freeze his own pay from increasing. While he may have indirectly benefited from the automatic pay adjustments, his votes can be seen as attempts to prevent a reduction in congressional salaries, rather than explicit votes to raise them.

journalist_explanation: Schultz said Christie firied 6,000 teachers. There are two problems with Schultz’s claim. First, the number is closer to 4,500, and even the teachers’ union would not say that all the people that held those jobs were fired. Some of them retired and were not replaced. The number of teachers declined but not necessarily through being fired or laid-off. Second, while Christie pushed hard for steep cuts to school funding, he also got help from local voters. Because of those caveats, we rate Schultz's claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that under Chris Christie's governorship, the number of teachers decreased by around 4,500 from 2010 to 2012. However, this is less than the claimed 6,000, and not all those teachers were directly fired. A spokesperson for the New Jersey Education Association stated that Christie backed a budget cut of $1.3 billion for schools, leading to a mix of layoffs and retirements, with more people laid off than retired. On the other hand, others argue that the responsibility for the loss of teachers rests solely on Christie's shoulders due to his cuts, while also pointing out that funding cuts were implemented in collaboration with the Democratic Legislature.

journalist_explanation: Huckabee said, "Only one out of five of the so-called ‘Syrian refugees’ who went into Europe were actually Syrian." While the claim isn’t pulled out of thin air, it’s flawed. The statistic represents the three months before the actual influx of Syrian refugees, and the four out of five non-Syrians are not purporting to be Syrian. Rather, they came from war-torn countries. Overall, Syrian refugees account for half of all refugees arriving in Europe in 2015 so far. We rate Huckabee’s claim Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The evidence suggests that Huckabee's claim is based on a flawed extrapolation of data from Eurostat, which only represents the situation in a three-month period before the Syrian migrants began arriving in bulk. According to Eurostat's quarterly report and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees' Syria page, asylum seekers from Syria represent half of all refugees when considering the whole picture.

journalist_explanation: Van de Putte said about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.That’s off by more than half; 588 Texans perished in action from January 2002 through the most recent Texan's death on Dec. 24, 2012, according to the federal government.The senator likely drew her number from the wrong column on a table. Regardless, what she said rates as False.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that the Department of Defense data indicates 588 Texans were killed in action since 9/11, contradicting Van de Putte's claim that only about 250 Texans have been killed in action during this time. This is confirmed by a table provided by the Defense Manpower Data Center and multiple officials involved in preparing the Senate committee's report on Van de Putte's proposal.

journalist_explanation: A chain e-mail circulating in New Jersey claims that Obama has "added" $6.5 trillion to the national debt, while his 43 predecessors added $6.3 trillion combined.But the chain e-mail is wrong to suggest the additional debt during Obama’s tenure already has exceeded the level of his predecessors. In terms of both debt held by the public and total debt, the Obama administration has added less debt than the amounts in place when he took office.Still, the national debt is projected to keep increasing. The amount of added debt held by the public may exceed Obama’s predecessors by October 2013, according to White House projections.We rate the statement Mostly False. To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while President Obama's administration is on track to add nearly $6.5 trillion to the national debt by October 2013, he has not yet added that much debt. Additionally, both forms of national debt had increased under his watch at a slower rate than the initial claim suggests.

journalist_explanation: Without Cantor, Maher said, the GOP in Congress is "now all Christian and all white except for one black senator, who was appointed." Maher’s show did not respond to a request for comment. If we learned anything from this fact-check, it is that straightforward sounding claims about religion and race are rarely that straightforward. Still, Maher’s unequivocal statement glosses over some diversity within the GOP’s ranks. On religion, Maher's claim comes down to how you view Mormonism. On race, the question is even more murky. There are two members of federally recognized American Indian tribes, which is classified as a race by the U.S. Census Bureau, and there are as many 10 Republicans in the House and Senate with Hispanic roots. Some may consider their race white,Hispanic or something else. Also, Cantor isn’t leaving office until the end of his term in January. It’s possible the November elections will bring non-Christian or non-white Republican members who will take office when Cantor leaves. Maher’s statement is partially accurarebut leaves out important details. We rate itHalf True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that while most Republicans in Congress identify as Christian or Protestant, there are exceptions such as Rep. Tulsi Gabbard (Hindu) and other non-Christian Democrats listed by the Pew Forum on Religion and Public Life report from 2012. However, regarding the claim of all white except for one appointed African-American official, while it is stated that there are no other African-American Republicans in Congress, the evidence also mentions Hispanic Republican senators and representatives, which could be interpreted as not "all white".

journalist_explanation: Menendez said Kyrillos "voted to raid the state's pension funds by $2.8 billion that is costing New Jersey taxpayers still today to the tune of nearly $15 billion dollars to repay that money."Kyrillos voted in favor of borrowing $2.75 billion to put into the state’s pension funds. The move allowed Whitman to avoid nearly $600 million in pension payments that year, but overall, money went into the system, not out of it. To call it a vote to raid pension funds by $2.8 billion is inaccurate.Also, the bonds will cost taxpayers, in total, about $10.1 billion, not $15 billion.We rate this claim False.To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: According to the evidence provided by PolitiFact New Jersey, Kyrillos voted for a plan that authorized the sale of $2.75 billion in bonds, which were deposited in state retirement funds and helped balance then-Gov. Christie Whitman's budget. While it is true that skipping payments into the pension system allowed Whitman to avoid making nearly $600 million in payments, this does not constitute a "raid" on the pension funds as Kyrillos put nearly $2.8 billion of borrowed money in the funds. Additionally, the state Treasury Department reports that the bonds will cost $10.1 billion to pay off, not nearly $15 billion.

journalist_explanation: Obama said, "A million people … could get health insurance right away" if Texas expanded Medicaid as encouraged by the Obamacare law. Estimates show some 1.4 million to 1.7 million would be eligible immediately. We rate his statement as True. TRUE – The statement is accurate and there’s nothing significant missing. Click here for more on the six PolitiFact ratings and how we select facts to check.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided quotes President Barack Obama stating "a million people" could get health insurance right away if Texas expanded Medicaid under Obamacare. Additionally, the state Health and Human Services Commission estimated that about 1 million adults were already on Medicaid in January 2013. Furthermore, other sources, such as the Urban Institute and Stephanie Goodman's statement, estimate that a significant number of Texans would become eligible for Medicaid if the state opted to expand, with figures ranging from approximately 1.4 million to 1.7 million. These estimates support President Obama's claim.

journalist_explanation: Christie said that "we created as many jobs in the first six months of this year as we did in all of 2011 and 2011 was the best single year for private-sector job growth since the year 2000."So far this year New Jersey added 39, 600 jobs in total. That’s 8,500 more jobs than the state gained in all of 2011.And in 2011, the state added more private-sector jobs than any year since 2000.The governor earns a True on this claim.To comment on this ruling, go to NJ.com.
generated_explanation: The evidence supports the claim that there were as many jobs created in the first six months of 2012 as in all of 2011 (39,600 total vs 31,100), and also supports the claim that 2011 was the best single year for private-sector job growth since the year 2000 with 33,400 new jobs.

journalist_explanation: Rubens said when armed civilians stop mass shootings with guns, an average of 2.5 people die; otherwise, an average of 18 people die. One of the most comprehensive studies of recent active shooter events suggests the average of 18 deaths when police stop the shooter is far too high. The study of more than 100 incidents determined the median number of people killed or wounded in all active shooter situations was five. The study documented only nine incidents out of dozens in which the number of people shot was 14 or higher. Conclusions about the number of deaths when an armed civilian takes action are also problematic because very limited data exists. The author of the study agrees it’s logical to assume casualties would be lower when civilians intervene before police arrive, but his research documented very few incidents that were actually stopped because a civilian was carrying a gun. Finally, both Rubens and the internet blogger who first offered the statistics that Rubens cited have acknowledged the figures were incorrect. Rubens has since revised his estimate to be in the range of 2.33 and 14. Overall, this statement is not accurate. We rate this claim False.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided presents conflicting information regarding the claim made by Jim Rubens. Initially, Rubens claimed that when armed civilians stop mass shootings with guns, an average of 2.5 people die; otherwise, an average of 18 people die. However, his campaign later acknowledged that these figures were incorrect and stood behind Davi Barker's revised calculations, which put the averages at 2.33 for incidents where civilians stop the shooter and 14.29 for incidents where police stop the shooter. In contrast, Dr. Pete Blair's academic study found that the median number of people shot in active shooter incidents is five (excluding the perpetrator) and that shooting incidents with death tolls above 18 are rare. Additionally, Blair pointed out problems with the terminology used by Rubens and emphasized that the data on armed civilians stopping active shooters is limited, making it difficult to draw conclusions about their effectiveness.

journalist_explanation: After a critical article was published about him last week, Tariq El-Shabazz released a statement Friday calling reporter Ryan Briggs racist and of publishing fake news. In his statement, El-Shabazz said the article had incorrectly claimed former client Anthony Brown was given a death sentence and that not a single client of his had ever been sentenced to death. Brown was not given the death penalty. He received a life sentence, andCity & State PAcorrected the error Monday. But a former client of El-Shabazz, Kaboni Savage, received a death sentence. El-Shabazz, however, did not represent Savage in the federal case that led to the sentence. Because he didn’t represent Savage in that case, a spokesperson for El-Shabazz said his claim stands as true. A former trial lawyer and expert on legal ethics agree. But while true in a legal sense, El-Shabazz’s statement needs clarification. We rule the claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that one of Tariq El-Shabazz's clients, Kaboni Savage, was given a federal death sentence for 12 counts of murder in 2013. Although El-Shabazz did not represent Savage during the federal case, he had previously represented him and was disqualified from representing him due to a conflict of interest. Therefore, it is not accurate for El-Shabazz to claim that none of his clients have ever been sentenced to death.

journalist_explanation: An ad from American Crossroads says, "This is what President Obama said the jobless rate would be if we passed the stimulus: 5.6 percent."But we find that's a stretch. In the evidence the group provided, Obama doesn’t mention that statistic. Rather, he introduced "projections" that included a chart showing the jobless rate falling to 5.6 percent under a recovery plan. The report highlighted the estimates’ "significant margins of error" and high uncertainty due to a recession that was "unusual both in its fundamental causes and its severity." The economy was, in fact, much worse than economists knew. The chart is now infamous, but it was never pitched as a promise. We rate the statement Mostly False.
generated_explanation: According to a January 9, 2009 report prepared for President-elect Obama, and his speech introducing the report, the jobless rate was projected to be around 5.6 percent in mid 2012 with a stimulus plan. The language used was cautious, referring to "projections" and warning about "significant margins of error."

journalist_explanation: Ernst said that "Iowa has the fourth fastest-growing personal income in the United States, while nationally, the real wage has decreased over the past eight years that Congressman Braley has been there by 2.7 percent." Iowa did rank fourth nationally in personal income growth, but only for the most recent quarter, and when compared to earlier quarters, this high rate seems like a statistical anomaly. Meanwhile, she’s wrong that real wages declined by 2.7 percent over the past eight years, although she does have a point that Iowa did somewhat better on this score than did the nation as a whole. Equally problematic, Ernst’s comparison between Iowa’s economy and the nation’s is questionable because it appears to compare quarterly data for one statistic to eight years of a different statistic. Economists say this isn’t a sound method. The claim contains an element of truth but ignores critical facts that would give a different impression, so we rate it Mostly False.
generated_explanation: The claim "Iowa has the fourth fastest-growing personal income in the United States" is supported by evidence from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, showing Iowa's 2.4% increase in personal income over the previous quarter in 2014 ranks fourth among all states, beating three other states including Nebraska and North Dakota. However, the evidence also suggests that this achievement may not be as significant as it seems when looking at longer periods of time, such as full-year periods from 2011 to 2013, which show Iowa ranking lower nationally in terms of percentage change in personal income. The claim "nationally, the real wage has decreased over the past eight years … by 2.7 percent" is disputed by evidence from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showing no significant decrease in median weekly earnings between 2006 and 2013.

journalist_explanation: There’s a slight snag in the first part of the Virginia Interfaith Center’s claim that, in 1968, a full- time minimum wage earner could support a household of three above the poverty line. The wage was bifurcated then. The majority earning $1.60 an hour could support a family of three, but a small group of workers qualifying for $1.15 an hour would have lived below the poverty line The second part of the center’s claim -- that a full-time worker today could not raise a family of two on the minimum wage of $7.25 an hour -- holds up. Clearly, the buying power of the minimum wage has decreased in recent decades. The center tried to illustrate that point with a statement that is accurate but needs a little clarification. So we rate its claim Mostly True.
generated_explanation: While evidence suggests that in 1968, a full-time worker earning minimum wage could support a family of three above the poverty line (given the correct hourly rate and calculation), it also shows that a small group of employees could be paid as little as $1.15 an hour, which would have fallen below the poverty line for a three-person household. Additionally, in modern times, it is stated that a full-time minimum wage earner makes $15,080 a year, which falls slightly below the average 2013 poverty threshold for a family of two ($15,156).

journalist_explanation: Northam said with decontamination systems being set up in Virginia, "PPE can be decontaminated and reused 20 times without degrading." The systems are excellent news for Virginia which, like practically all states, has struggled to acquire N95 masks for medical workers. But the governor’s words are still rosy. The FDA, in its letter of emergency approval, said the decontamination system "may be effective" safely recycling masks up to 20 times, but warned the process should only be used when there are "insufficient (new) supplies." Some early research suggests the structure of the masks may be compromised through the repeated process, making them less-secure fits on faces. So Northam’s statement is partially accurate, but leaves out important details. We rate it Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provided shows that the Battelle Memorial Institute's decontamination systems can effectively clean N95 face masks up to 20 times without degrading their performance, allowing them to be reused multiple times. This is confirmed by Governor Northam's statement and supported by technical details from the FDA and expert opinions, although it is noted that this method should only be used as a crisis measure due to limitations in research and variability in mask effectiveness.

journalist_explanation: Rubio said that "for the first time in 35 years, we have more businesses dying than we do starting." The change didn’t happen in the past year or two -- it occurred in 2008 -- but in general, Rubio has accurately cited a statistic from a respected think tank’s report. The co-author of that report said he feels Rubio has stated the claim accurately. We rate Rubio’s claim True.
generated_explanation: The Brookings Institution's 2014 report, titled "Declining Business Dynamism in the United States," provides data from the Business Dynamics Statistics that supports Rubio's claim. According to the report, the entry rate of new firms declined by nearly half between 1978 and 2011, and for the first time in the 30-plus-year history of the data, business deaths now exceed business births. This is further confirmed by Litan, one of the coauthors of the report, who stated that Rubio's claim is accurate.

journalist_explanation: The Save My Care ad says that Curbelo voted for a health care bill that will let insurance companies "charge five times more for people over 50." The ad refers to a provision that will allow insurance companies to charge adults five times more for insurance than younger people buying on the individual market. But the ad could leave a misleading impression that it’s five times more than the current situation -- and that’s not the case. Under the Affordable Care Act, insurers were allowed to charge this age group three times as much for insurance (which was considered a better deal than the situation before). Also, the increase in the ratio applies to Americans ages 50-64 -- not seniors who are on Medicare. We rate this claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence shows that under current law, insurance companies can charge older adults up to three times as much as younger people. However, the House bill increases this ratio up to five times starting in 2018, unless states set a different age ratio. This means that if the House bill were to become law, older adults would pay more for health insurance compared to current law.

journalist_explanation: Gingrich said that "gangs have increased by 40 percent since this president was elected." Gingrich deserves credit for using statistics from a credible federal agency, but it’s important to note that methodological difficulties make it hard for anyone, even the FBI, to determine how many gang members there are in the United States. Criminologists express skepticism about whether gang membership could have jumped 40 percent in just two years, saying that broader crime statistics don’t show any sign of it. In addition, despite the Gingrich camp’s insistence that he did not mean to cast blame on Obama for the rise in gang membership, we think that a reasonable viewer of the discussion could have made such an inference. On balance, we rate the claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The evidence provides both support and criticism of Gingrich's claim that gangs have increased by 40 percent since this president was elected. On one hand, the FBI study quoted by Gingrich in his op-ed does show a 40 percent increase in gang members from 2009 to 2011. However, experts and criminologists raise several concerns about the reliability of these statistics, including uncertainty about the survey's sample size and accuracy, potential for institutional bias, and the difficulty of defining who counts as a gang member. They also point out that crime rates have not increased significantly in this period, which contradicts the idea of a 40 percent increase in gang activity.

journalist_explanation: Sanders said, "Puerto Rico’s $70 billion debt is unsustainable and it is unpayable. And the reason why it is unsustainable has everything to do with the greed of Wall Street vulture funds." Puerto Rico’s debt was already unsustainable by the time Wall Street hedge funds and banks began playing a role as a result of decades of local mismanagement, U.S. policy and economic misfortune. But Sanders has a point that the financial sector has taken advantage of and is excerbating the situation. What's more, they're effectively preventing crisis relief byactively working to stop Puerto Rico from restructuring its debt. We rate his claim Half True.
generated_explanation: The claim that Puerto Rico's $70 billion debt is unsustainable and unpayable due to the greed of Wall Street vulture funds has some truth, but it is not entirely accurate. While it is true that Puerto Rico's debt is unsustainable and Wall Street has profited from it, the evidence suggests that the debt was accumulating long before Wall Street got involved. The island's debt is attributed to a combination of US policy, local mismanagement, economic decline, and poor management decisions made by the government over the years. While Wall Street has certainly exacerbated the situation and is benefiting from it, they did not cause the problem alone.

journalist_explanation: Make no mistake: Crist is ripe for attacks about flip-flopping. We've already pretty much written a book about it, noting that his position on oil drilling has shifted, as has his position on the federal health care bill.
